derivations.claim: For $z\in D$, its definition gives $z=a/2^r$ for some $a\in O$ and integer $r\ge0$. Expand $a$ in the integral basis [F1]. Among all such exponents choose the least $r$; if $r>0$ and all four coefficients of $a$ were even, replacing $(a,r)$ by $(a/2,r-1)$ would contradict minimality. This gives an encoding of the required form.

Suppose $a/2^r=b/2^s$ are two canonical encodings. If $r<s$, then $b=2^{s-r}a$, so every coefficient of $b$ is even, contrary to its canonical condition because $s>0$. If $s<r$, the same argument makes every coefficient of $a$ even. Hence $r=s$, and then $a=b$; uniqueness of the four coefficients follows from the basis property [F1]. The zero element is represented only by the all-zero numerator, and minimality forces its exponent to be $0$.

Set $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$, $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$, and
$D=O[1/2]=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$. The relation $\omega^4=-1$ reduces every
element of $O$ to four integer coefficients in the power basis
$1,\omega,\omega^2,\omega^3$. The canonical dyadic encoding of a nonzero
$z\in D$ is

$$z=(a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3)/2^r,$$

where $r\ge0$ is least and, if $r>0$, the four integers are not all even.
Zero is encoded with $r=0$ and all four coefficients zero. Arithmetic is exact:
multiply polynomials, reduce with $\omega^4=-1$, combine denominators, and
remove the common power of $2$ from the coefficients. The integral-basis
supplier [[thm-cyclotomic-ring-of-integers]] and the proof of
[[lem-qc-dyadic-coefficient-encoding]] justify existence and uniqueness.

derivations.claim: Multiplying $(\omega-\omega^3)(a+b\omega+c\omega^2+d\omega^3)$ and reducing every power $\omega^j$ with $\omega^4=-1$ gives $(b-d)+(a+c)\omega+(b+d)\omega^2+(c-a)\omega^3$. By [F1], this product is in $2O$ exactly when all four displayed coefficients are even, which is equivalent to $a+c$ and $b+d$ even, or $a\equiv c$ and $b\equiv d\pmod2$. This proves the first criterion.

Expanding $x\bar x$ with $\bar\omega=-\omega^3$ and reducing powers gives the stated $P+\sqrt2Q$. Write $A=a+c$ and $B=b+d$ modulo $2$. Then $P\equiv A+B$ and $Q\equiv AB\pmod2$. The pair $(A+B,AB)$ is $(0,0)$ exactly for $(A,B)=(0,0)$: the other three pairs give $(0,1)$, $(1,0)$, or $(1,0)$. Since $P+\sqrt2Q$ is in $2O$ exactly when its unique power-basis coefficients are all even, equivalently when $P,Q$ are both even, the norm is in $2O$ exactly when $A=B=0$, which by step 1.1 is exactly when $\sqrt2$ divides $x$.

derivations.claim: Since $(\sqrt2)^{2r}=2^r$, multiplying $z$ by $(\sqrt2)^{2r}$ gives its canonical numerator in $O$. Hence the exponent set is nonempty.

Suppose $k=-m<0$ belongs to that set, so $z=(\sqrt2)^m y$ for some $y\in O$. Then the numerator $a=2^rz=(\sqrt2)^{m+2r}y=2^q(\sqrt2)^\epsilon y$, where $q=\lfloor(m+2r)/2\rfloor$ and $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}$. Multiplication by $\sqrt2$ has integer coefficients in the power basis, so all coefficients of $a$ are divisible by $2^q$. Choose a nonzero coefficient $a_j$; its finite $2$-adic valuation bounds $q$ above, and therefore bounds $m$ above. Thus the negative exponents in the set are bounded below; nonnegative exponents already are.
A nonempty subset of $\mathbb Z$ bounded below has a least element. Hence the set of clearing exponents has a least integer; this does not assume that the least exponent is nonnegative.

Every $z\in D$ has exactly one canonical dyadic encoding specified in
[[def-qc-dyadic-cyclotomic-ring]].

For $x=a+b\omega+c\omega^2+d\omega^3\in O$, multiplication by
$\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ has coefficient vector
$(b-d,a+c,b+d,c-a)$. Consequently $\sqrt2$ divides $x$ in $O$ exactly when
$a\equiv c$ and $b\equiv d\pmod2$. Also,

$$x\bar x=P+\sqrt2Q,\qquad P=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2,\quad Q=a(b-d)+c(b+d),$$

and $2$ divides $x\bar x$ in $O$ exactly when $\sqrt2$ divides $x$.

derivations.claim: For nonzero $z$, write its canonical form $z=a/2^r$ using [F1]. If $r>0$, then $a\bar a=2^{2r}$, so $2\mid a\bar a$ in $O$ and [F2] gives $a=\sqrt2a_1$ for some $a_1\in O$. Whenever $a_j\in O$ has $a_j\bar a_j=2^m$ with $m>0$, the same argument gives $a_j=\sqrt2a_{j+1}$ and $a_{j+1}\bar a_{j+1}=2^{m-1}$. Applying this for $m=2r,2r-1,\ldots,1$ yields $a=(\sqrt2)^{2r}a_{2r}=2^ra_{2r}$. All canonical coefficients of $a$ are then even, contradicting the minimality of $r$. Thus $r=0$ and $z\in O$.

Write $z=a+b\omega+c\omega^2+d\omega^3$ with integer coefficients. Direct multiplication gives $z\bar z=P+\sqrt2Q=1$, where $P=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$ and $Q=a(b-d)+c(b+d)$ by [F2]. The numbers $1$ and $\sqrt2$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$: if $\sqrt2=m/n$ in lowest terms, then $m^2=2n^2$ forces $m$ even and then $n$ even, a contradiction. Thus $P=1$ and $Q=0$. Four integer squares sum to $1$ only when exactly one coefficient is $1$ or $-1$ and the others are zero. Hence $z\in\{\pm1,\pm\omega,\pm\omega^2,\pm\omega^3\}=\{\omega^j:0\le j<8\}$.

Set $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$, $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$, and
$D=O[1/2]=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$. The relation $\omega^4=-1$ reduces every
element of $O$ to four integer coefficients in the power basis
$1,\omega,\omega^2,\omega^3$. The canonical dyadic encoding of a nonzero
$z\in D$ is

$$z=(a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3)/2^r,$$

where $r\ge0$ is least and, if $r>0$, the four integers are not all even.
Zero is encoded with $r=0$ and all four coefficients zero. Arithmetic is exact:
multiply polynomials, reduce with $\omega^4=-1$, combine denominators, and
remove the common power of $2$ from the coefficients. The integral-basis
supplier [[thm-cyclotomic-ring-of-integers]] and the proof of
[[lem-qc-dyadic-coefficient-encoding]] justify existence and uniqueness.

Let $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, where $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The class $[5]_8$ is a
unit modulo $8$, so the cyclotomic Galois group supplier
[[cor-the-galois-group-of-a-rational-cyclotomic-field]] gives the unique
$\mathbb Q$-automorphism $\bullet$ with
$\omega^\bullet=\omega^5=-\omega$. It fixes $i=\omega^2$ and sends
$\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ to $-\sqrt2$. Complex conjugation and $\bullet$
commute, as is checked on the generator $\omega$. The four embeddings of $K$
are the identity, complex conjugation, $\bullet$, and their composite,
because the Galois group consists of the four maps $\omega\mapsto\omega^j$
for $j=1,3,5,7$. Since $\bullet$ fixes $1/2$ and maps $\omega$ into
$\mathbb Z[\omega]$, it preserves $D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$.

This is the nontrivial real-conjugation embedding used in the scaled-grid
conditions; it is distinct from complex conjugation.

Let $D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$ and
$D_+=\mathbb Z[\sqrt2,1/2]\subseteq\mathbb R$. For every $z\in D$, its
complex-conjugate norm satisfies $z^\dagger z\in D_+$. More precisely, if
$z=(a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3)/2^r$ is its canonical encoding,
then
$$z^\dagger z=\frac{P+\sqrt2Q}{2^{2r}},\quad P=\sum_{j=0}^3a_j^2,\quad Q=a_0(a_1-a_3)+a_2(a_1+a_3).$$

derivations.claim: The two inequalities $|u|,|u^\bullet|\le1$, together with their complex conjugates, give $|\sigma_j(u)|\le1$ for all four embeddings $j=1,3,5,7$; these are the identity, complex conjugation, $\bullet$, and their composite by [F2]. If $k=-m<0$, the definition of $k$ gives $x=(\sqrt2)^k u=(\sqrt2)^{-m}u\in O$, so $u=(\sqrt2)^m x$. Thus $|\sigma_j(x)|\le2^{-m/2}$ for every $j$. By [F3], $x\bar x=P+\sqrt2Q$ with $P,Q\in\mathbb Z$. Since $\bullet$ negates $\sqrt2$ and commutes with conjugation, the product of all four embeddings is $\prod_{j=1,3,5,7}\sigma_j(x)=(x\bar x)(x^\bullet\overline{x^\bullet})=(P+\sqrt2Q)(P-\sqrt2Q)=P^2-2Q^2$. It is a nonzero integer because $x\ne0$ and each embedding is injective. Its modulus is at most $2^{-2m}<1$, a contradiction. This proves $k\ge0$.

For $k\ge0$, set $a=(\sqrt2)^ku\in O$. Then $|\sigma_j(a)|\le2^{k/2}$ for every $j$. Fourier inversion in the power basis gives $a_r=\frac14\sum_{j\in\{1,3,5,7\}}\sigma_j(a)\omega^{-jr}$: expanding the sum, the coefficient of $a_s$ is $\frac14\sum_{j\text{ odd}}\omega^{j(s-r)}$, which equals $1$ for $s=r$ and $0$ for distinct $r,s\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. Therefore $|a_r|\le\frac14\sum_j|\sigma_j(a)|\le2^{k/2}$. Since $a_r$ is an integer, it lies in the stated finite interval.

For $x=a+b\omega+c\omega^2+d\omega^3\in O$, multiplication by
$\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ has coefficient vector
$(b-d,a+c,b+d,c-a)$. Consequently $\sqrt2$ divides $x$ in $O$ exactly when
$a\equiv c$ and $b\equiv d\pmod2$. Also,

$$x\bar x=P+\sqrt2Q,\qquad P=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2,\quad Q=a(b-d)+c(b+d),$$

and $2$ divides $x\bar x$ in $O$ exactly when $\sqrt2$ divides $x$.

derivations.claim: Put $s=\operatorname{sde}(z)$ and $x=(\sqrt2)^s z\in O$. Minimality of $s$ implies $\sqrt2\nmid x$, since otherwise $x=\sqrt2 y$ with $y\in O$ would make $(\sqrt2)^{s-1}z=y\in O$.

Write $x=a+b\omega+c\omega^2+d\omega^3$ and set $A=a+c$, $B=b+d$. By [F1], $\sqrt2\nmid x$ means $(A,B)$ is not $(0,0)$ modulo $2$. The two congruences $P\equiv A+B$ and $Q\equiv AB$ show that $P,Q$ are not both even: among the three nonzero pairs $(A,B)\in\{0,1\}^2$, the pair $(A+B,AB)$ is never $(0,0)$. For $P+\sqrt2Q$, divisibility by $(\sqrt2)^2=2$ is equivalent to both coefficients $P,Q$ being even. Hence $x\bar x$ is divisible by $\sqrt2$ at most once.

Let $m\in\{0,1\}$ be the number of factors $\sqrt2$ dividing $x\bar x$; write $x\bar x=(\sqrt2)^m y$ with $y\in O$ and $\sqrt2\nmid y$. Since $|z|^2=(x\bar x)/(\sqrt2)^{2s}$, its least denominator exponent is $2s-m$: multiplying by that power gives $y$, while any smaller exponent leaves a denominator because $\sqrt2\nmid y$. Thus $\operatorname{sde}(|z|^2)=2s-m$.
The hypothesis gives $2s-m\le3$ and $m\le1$, so $2s\le4$ and $s\le2$.

Set $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$, $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$, and
$D=O[1/2]=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$. The relation $\omega^4=-1$ reduces every
element of $O$ to four integer coefficients in the power basis
$1,\omega,\omega^2,\omega^3$. The canonical dyadic encoding of a nonzero

$$z=(a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3)/2^r,$$

where $r\ge0$ is least and, if $r>0$, the four integers are not all even.

remove the common power of $2$ from the coefficients. The integral-basis
supplier [[thm-cyclotomic-ring-of-integers]] and the proof of
[[lem-qc-dyadic-coefficient-encoding]] justify existence and uniqueness.

Let $n\ge r\ge1$, let $w=(w_0,\ldots,w_{r-1})$ be an ordered tuple of distinct wires in $[n]$, and let $U:\mathcal Q_r\to\mathcal Q_r$ be unitary. There is a unique unitary $\widetilde U_w:\mathcal Q_n\to\mathcal Q_n$ that applies $U$ to the ordered wires $w_0,\ldots,w_{r-1}$ and acts as the identity on the other wires.

For a gate occurrence $g=(\gamma,w)$ in a circuit on $\mathcal Q_n$, let $\widetilde U_g$ be the global embedding from [[lem-qc-local-gate-wire-embedding]]. For a layer $L_t=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$, define
$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$
For a circuit with chronological layers $L_1,\ldots,L_d$, define
$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

derivations.claim: Since $1/\sqrt2=\sqrt2/2=(\omega-\omega^3)/2\in D$, every entry of $H$ lies in $D$. The displayed diagonal gates have entries $0$ or powers of $\omega$, the scalar Clifford phases have entries powers of $\omega$, and the displayed CNOT has entries $0$ or $1$, so each primitive gate matrix has entries in $D$ by [F1] and [F2]. The embeddings in [F3] are obtained from tensoring with identity matrices and permuting factors; these operations only insert zeros and copy entries, hence preserve membership in $D$.

The product of two matrices with entries in a subring has entries that are finite sums of products in that subring. By the finite product interpretation [F4], induction on the circuit's finite gate list therefore places every entry of its matrix in $D$; the empty word is the identity matrix and also has entries in $D$.

consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

derivations.claim: By [F7], determinant is a homomorphism on $G$, and [F2] places its image in the finite group $\mu_8$. Therefore its kernel $G_1=\{W\in G:\det W=1\}$ has finite index in $G$. Let $\pi:U(2)\to PU(2)$ be the quotient map. Then $\pi(G_1)$ has finite index in $\pi(G)$, and [F1] makes $\pi(G)$ dense. Its closure $\overline{\pi(G_1)}$ is consequently a closed finite-index subgroup of $PU(2)$: the dense group $\pi(G)$ is a finite union of cosets of $\pi(G_1)$, so its closure is the same finite union of the corresponding closed cosets of $\overline{\pi(G_1)}$. Every projective class has an $SU(2)$ representative: write $\det Q=e^{i\phi}$ using [F8] and multiply $Q$ by $\lambda=e^{-i\phi/2}$. Every $SU(2)$ matrix has eigenvalues $e^{i\alpha},e^{-i\alpha}$; [F4] diagonalizes it and the path $s\mapsto S\operatorname{diag}(e^{is\alpha}, e^{-is\alpha})S^*$ joins it to $I$. Thus $SU(2)$, and hence its continuous image $PU(2)$, is connected. The complement of a finite-index closed subgroup is a finite union of its closed cosets, so that subgroup is also open. Since $PU(2)$ is connected, its only nonempty clopen subgroup is $PU(2)$ itself; hence $\overline{\pi(G_1)}=PU(2)$.

Choose $\delta>0$ and, by the density just proved, a word $W\in G_1$ and a scalar $|\lambda|=1$ with $\|W-\lambda R\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\delta$. Write the columns of $W$ and $R$ as $w_1,w_2$ and $r_1,r_2$. Multilinearity [F5] gives $\det W-\det(\lambda R)=\det(w_1-\lambda r_1,w_2) +\det(\lambda r_1,w_2-\lambda r_2)$. For $x=(x_1,x_2)^T$ and $y=(y_1,y_2)^T$, expanding both sides gives $|\det(x,y)|^2=\|x\|^2\|y\|^2-|\langle x,y\rangle|^2 =|x_1|^2|y_2|^2+|x_2|^2|y_1|^2-2\operatorname{Re}(x_1y_2\bar x_2\bar y_1) \le\|x\|^2\|y\|^2$. Since the columns are unit vectors and each column difference has norm less than $\delta$ by [F6], $|1-\lambda^2|\le2\delta$.

Put $a=|\lambda-1|$ and $b=|\lambda+1|$. Then $a^2+b^2=4$ and $ab=|1-\lambda^2|\le2\delta$. Since $\max(a,b)\ge\sqrt2$ from $a^2+b^2=4$, we have $\min(a,b)=ab/\max(a,b)\le\sqrt2\,\delta$. Choose $\sigma\in\{1,-1\}$ attaining this minimum. By the triangle inequality and $\|R\|_{\mathrm{op}}=1$, $\|W-\sigma R\|_{\mathrm{op}}< (1+\sqrt2)\delta$. The scalar $-I$ is a word in $G$: direct multiplication gives $$X=HZH=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad XZ=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad (XZ)^2=-I.$$ Thus $\sigma W\in G_1$, and $\|\sigma W-R\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|W-\sigma R\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ is less than $(1+\sqrt2)\delta$. Because $\det(-I)=1$ and $\det W=1$, this scalar correction leaves the determinant equal to $1$. Choosing $\delta<\varepsilon/(1+\sqrt2)$ proves the claim.

For $\theta\in\mathbb R$ set
$R_z(\theta)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{-i\theta/2},e^{i\theta/2})$. Given
$\varepsilon>0$, the on-the-nose ancilla-free approximation problem is to
find a finite one-qubit Clifford+T word $U$ such that

$$\|R_z(\theta)-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon,$$

and minimize the number of occurrences of $T$ or $T^\dagger$; the $T$-count
of a word is this integer. An overall scalar Clifford phase $\omega^j I$,
viewed under [[def-qc-global-phase-equivalence]], is free in the resource
count but remains part of the exact matrix used in the displayed norm
inequality. Thus changing the representative can change feasibility even
when it leaves T-count unchanged. No workspace wire is
permitted. The operator norm is the finite-dimensional norm from
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].

This defines a mathematical optimization problem for exact real inputs
$(\theta,\varepsilon)$. It does not specify a bit representation or assert a
Turing algorithm for arbitrary real input.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a bijection from $[0,2\pi)$ onto $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

derivations.claim: Put $\Delta=R_z(\theta)^*U$. It is unitary and has determinant $1$, so [F2] diagonalizes it. Its eigenvalues $\lambda,\mu$ have modulus one by unitarity and satisfy $\lambda\mu=1$ by the determinant, hence $\mu=\bar\lambda$. By [F4], write $\lambda=e^{it}$ with $t\in[0,2\pi)$; if $t>\pi$, swap $\lambda,\mu$ and put $\alpha=2\pi-t$, while if $t\le\pi$ put $\alpha=t$. Thus the eigenvalues are $e^{i\alpha},e^{-i\alpha}$ for some $\alpha\in[0,\pi]$. From the displayed matrices, $\operatorname{tr}\Delta=e^{i\theta/2}u+e^{-i\theta/2}\bar u =2\operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)$. Hence $\cos\alpha= \operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)$.

Left multiplication by $R_z(\theta)^*$ preserves vector norms, so [F3] gives $\|R_z(\theta)-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|I-\Delta\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. Let $S$ be a unitary diagonalizer of $\Delta$ from [F2]; conjugation by $S$ preserves the operator norm by [F3]. Using [F4] then gives $\|I-\Delta\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2 =\max(|1-e^{i\alpha}|^2,|1-e^{-i\alpha}|^2) =2-2\cos\alpha =2-2\operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)$. Both the operator norm and $\varepsilon$ are nonnegative, so squaring the bound is equivalent to the stated real-part inequality.

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

Input two data bits $a,b$ and a third clean work bit $t=0$. On the ordered
register $(a,b,t)$, apply the following chronological word:

1. $H_t$.
2. $\operatorname{CNOT}_{b,t},T_t^\dagger,\operatorname{CNOT}_{a,t},T_t,
   \operatorname{CNOT}_{b,t},T_t^\dagger,\operatorname{CNOT}_{a,t}$.
3. $T_b,T_t,H_t$.
4. $\operatorname{CNOT}_{a,b},T_a,T_b^\dagger,\operatorname{CNOT}_{a,b}$.
5. $T_t$.
6. Apply the same 15-gate word from steps 1–4 again.

The 15-gate word in steps 1–4 is the specified three-wire block. The output
is the complete three-wire circuit, with no implicit fourth wire.

Let $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The one-qubit generators and exact matrices in the
ordered computational basis are

$$H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega\end{pmatrix},\qquad T^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$

On basis vectors, $H|q\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^q|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and
$T^k|q\rangle=\omega^{kq}|q\rangle$ for $q\in\{0,1\}$.

Write $S=T^2=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)$ and
$Z=T^4=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. Pauli $X,Y,Z$ are as in
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]]. On two ordered wires,
$\operatorname{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,b\mathbin\oplus a\rangle$; the first wire
is control and the second target. A circuit is a finite chronological word of
these gates at stated wire positions; its matrix is the product with later
gates on the left. No extra wire or controlled-$T$ operation is implicit.

The scalar phase $\omega I$ is an allowed Clifford phase in the one-qubit
matrix-word convention. Its scalar factor is retained in exact matrix products;
the convention that an overall scalar does not affect a resource count is
stated separately from matrix equality. It does not grant a controlled-$T$
operation or allow a scalar on a target wire to be discarded under control.

The exact one-qubit H/T algebra is generated by $H,T,T^\dagger$; $S$ and $Z$
are aliases for the displayed powers. The distinction between exact matrix
equality and [[def-qc-global-phase-equivalence|global-phase equivalence]] is
maintained. Resource costs are supplied by
[[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]] and remain separate from this matrix
definition.

For a gate occurrence $g=(\gamma,w)$ in a circuit on $\mathcal Q_n$, let $\widetilde U_g$ be the global embedding from [[lem-qc-local-gate-wire-embedding]]. For a layer $L_t=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$, define
$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$
For a circuit with chronological layers $L_1,\ldots,L_d$, define
$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

Let $n\ge r\ge1$, let $w=(w_0,\ldots,w_{r-1})$ be an ordered tuple of distinct wires in $[n]$, and let $U:\mathcal Q_r\to\mathcal Q_r$ be unitary. There is a unique unitary $\widetilde U_w:\mathcal Q_n\to\mathcal Q_n$ that applies $U$ to the ordered wires $w_0,\ldots,w_{r-1}$ and acts as the identity on the other wires.

Let $C=\mathbb C^2$ be a control qubit with ordered orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $U:H\to H$ be unitary. On the control-first register $C\otimes H$, define

$$C(U):=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus $C(U)(|0\rangle\otimes v)=|0\rangle\otimes v$ and $C(U)(|1\rangle\otimes v)=|1\rangle\otimes Uv$. **Controlled access** means that the chosen operation model explicitly grants a call to this block operator. An ordinary call to a black-box $U$ does not silently grant a controlled call, and no query or gate cost is assigned unless the model states it.

Let $D$ be a finite ordered quantum register and let $A$ be an ordered register of $k\ge0$ ancilla qubits, with Hilbert spaces $\mathcal H_D$ and $\mathcal H_A$. Write $|0_A\rangle=|0^k\rangle$, including $|0_A\rangle=1$ when $k=0$. Let $U$ be a unitary on $\mathcal H_D\otimes\mathcal H_A$ and let $V$ be a unitary on $\mathcal H_D$.

The register $A$ is a **clean ancilla register for $U$ and $V$** when
$$
U(|\psi\rangle_D\otimes|0_A\rangle)=V|\psi\rangle_D\otimes|0_A\rangle
$$
for every vector $|\psi\rangle_D$. Thus the data operation is independent of the input vector and all clean wires return exactly to zero.

The register $A$ is a **dirty ancilla register for $U$ and $V$** when the operator identity $U=V\otimes I_A$ holds on $\mathcal H_D\otimes\mathcal H_A$. Equivalently, every product input $|\psi\rangle_D\otimes|\eta\rangle_A$ is mapped to $V|\psi\rangle_D\otimes|\eta\rangle_A$, with the same $V$ for every data and ancilla vector. This requires exact restoration of an arbitrary, initially unknown ancilla state and forbids residual data–ancilla correlation.

These are exact contracts for the complete subroutine. A temporary intermediate alteration of an ancilla is permitted if the full unitary satisfies the stated identity.

All bits are in $\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}$, with addition denoted by $\oplus$ and multiplication by juxtaposition. On three distinct ordered computational-basis wires, define the Toffoli gate $T$ and Fredkin gate $F$ by
$$
T|a,b,t\rangle=|a,b,t\oplus ab\rangle,
$$
and
$$
F|0,a,b\rangle=|0,a,b\rangle,\qquad F|1,a,b\rangle=|1,b,a\rangle.
$$
These basis actions extend linearly. Wire order is exactly the order displayed; the first two wires of $T$ are controls and the third is its target, while the first wire of $F$ is its control and the other two are conditionally swapped. Negative-control variants mean conjugating the chosen positive control by $X$ before and after the gate. These are fixed arity-three labels in the declared finite gate alphabet, not implicit access to arbitrary multicontrol gates. Their reversibility is established in [[lem-qc-x-cnot-toffoli-and-fredkin-are-involutions]].

derivations.claim: Fix the controls $a,b$ and let $q$ be the target bit immediately after the first $H_t$. The seven phase gates in [F1] contribute exponent $E_{a,b}(q)=-(q\oplus b)+(q\oplus a\oplus b)-(q\oplus a)+b+q\pmod8$. For $(a,b)=00,01,10,11$, the pairs $(E(0),E(1))$ are respectively $(0,0),(1,1),(0,0),(7,3)$. Conjugating these diagonal phases by the final $H_t$ therefore gives, for the four control values, $I,\omega I,I,\omega^7X$ on the target. The last CNOT–$T_a$–$T_b^\dagger$–CNOT block contributes data phase $\omega^{a-(a\oplus b)}$, which is $1,\omega^{-1},1,\omega$ in the same order. The combined action is exactly $|a,b,t\rangle\mapsto|a,b,t\oplus ab\rangle$ with phase $1$ in all eight cases, proving the displayed word is Toffoli in the sense of [F7]. By [F3,F4], these basis actions give the denotational matrix of the displayed chronological circuit.

Starting with $t=0$, the first Toffoli sends $|a,b,0\rangle$ to $|a,b,ab\rangle$. The middle $T_t$ multiplies this vector by $\omega^{ab}$; applying the Toffoli action [F7] again gives target $ab\oplus ab=0$. Thus the full circuit sends each basis vector to $\omega^{ab}|a,b,0\rangle$. The matrix product is the chronological circuit action by [F3,F4].

Every vector on data and a finite-dimensional reference with a clean ancilla has the finite expansion $\sum_{a,b,r}c_{abr}|a,b,r\rangle|0\rangle$. Applying step 2.1 termwise gives $\sum_{a,b,r}c_{abr}\omega^{ab}|a,b,r\rangle|0\rangle$, which is $C(T)$ on the data and identity on the reference, tensored with the restored zero state, by [F5,F6]. This is the asserted correlated-input action.

derivations.claim: By [F6], the two one-wire embeddings are $H\otimes I_2,I_2\otimes H$ and the corresponding tensor embeddings for $T,T^\dagger,S,S^\dagger,X,Y,Z$ and scalar phases. Direct diagonal/permutation calculations give $\det(H\otimes I_2)=\det(I_2\otimes H)=1$, $\det(T\otimes I_2)=\det(I_2\otimes T)=\omega^2$, and $\det(T^\dagger\otimes I_2)=\det(I_2\otimes T^\dagger)=\omega^{-2}$. The same calculation gives determinant $\omega^4$ for embedded $S,S^\dagger$, determinant $1$ for embedded $X,Y,Z$, and $\omega^{4j}$ for the embedded scalar phase $\omega^jI_2$. CNOT is a single transposition of $|10\rangle$ and $|11\rangle$, so its determinant is $-1=\omega^4$. Thus every primitive determinant is an even power of $\omega$; [F4,F7] make the determinant of a finite circuit product an even power as well.

citations.quote:
Every exact one-qubit Clifford+T matrix word, including a free scalar
Clifford phase $\omega^j I$, has determinant in
$\{\omega^k:k\in\mathbb Z\}$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

For square matrices $U,V$ of the same size, write $U\sim_{\mathrm{phase}}V$ when $U=\lambda V$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ with $|\lambda|=1$. This relation is kept distinct from exact matrix equality.

For $\theta\in\mathbb R$ set
$R_z(\theta)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{-i\theta/2},e^{i\theta/2})$. Given
$\varepsilon>0$, the on-the-nose ancilla-free approximation problem is to
find a finite one-qubit Clifford+T word $U$ such that

$$\|R_z(\theta)-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon,$$

and minimize the number of occurrences of $T$ or $T^\dagger$; the $T$-count
of a word is this integer. An overall scalar Clifford phase $\omega^j I$,
viewed under [[def-qc-global-phase-equivalence]], is free in the resource
count but remains part of the exact matrix used in the displayed norm
inequality. Thus changing the representative can change feasibility even
when it leaves T-count unchanged. No workspace wire is
permitted. The operator norm is the finite-dimensional norm from
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].

This defines a mathematical optimization problem for exact real inputs
$(\theta,\varepsilon)$. It does not specify a bit representation or assert a
Turing algorithm for arbitrary real input.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional target space, let $U$ be unitary on $H$, and let $|\lambda|=1$. In control-first order put
$$C(U)=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix},\qquad P_\lambda=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\lambda\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then $C(\lambda U)=(P_\lambda\otimes I_H)C(U)$. A scalar multiplying an entire output leaves every defined finite-POVM outcome law unchanged, whereas a scalar attached to a target matrix inside a control gives a phase on only the active control block; applying $P_{\overline\lambda}$ on the control restores the exact controlled matrix.

Let $C=\mathbb C^2$ be a control qubit with ordered orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $U:H\to H$ be unitary. On the control-first register $C\otimes H$, define

$$C(U):=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus $C(U)(|0\rangle\otimes v)=|0\rangle\otimes v$ and $C(U)(|1\rangle\otimes v)=|1\rangle\otimes Uv$. **Controlled access** means that the chosen operation model explicitly grants a call to this block operator. An ordinary call to a black-box $U$ does not silently grant a controlled call, and no query or gate cost is assigned unless the model states it.

The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a bijection from $[0,2\pi)$ onto $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

derivations.claim: Write $\det U=\omega^k$ by [F1], and set $V=e^{-ik\pi/8}R^*U$. Since $\det R=1$, [F4] gives $\det V=e^{-ik\pi/4}\omega^k=1$. The unitary $V$ is normal, so [F2] diagonalizes it. Its two eigenvalues have product $1$ and modulus $1$, hence are $e^{i\phi},e^{-i\phi}$ for some $\phi$ by [F9]; consequently $\operatorname{tr}V=2\cos\phi$ is real. Choose $\sigma\in\{1,-1\}$ such that $W=\sigma V$ has nonnegative trace. Since $-1=e^{i8\pi/8}$, $W=e^{in\pi/8}R^*U$ for an integer $n$, and $W$ is unitary with determinant $1$.

Since $W\in SU(2)$, its eigenvalues are a unit scalar and its conjugate; by [F9] write them $e^{it},e^{-it}$ and, swapping them if needed, choose $\alpha\in[0,\pi]$ with eigenvalues $e^{i\alpha},e^{-i\alpha}$. Then $\operatorname{tr}W=2\cos\alpha\ge0$; [F10,F11] imply $\alpha\le\pi/2$. For any unit scalar $\mu$, choose its angle $t\in[0,2\pi)$ by [F9] and set $\psi=t$ if $t\le\pi$, or $\psi=t-2\pi$ otherwise. Thus $\psi\in[-\pi,\pi]$. By [F2] and [F3], $\|I-W\|_{\mathrm{op}}=|1-e^{i\alpha}|$ and $\|I-\mu W\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\max\{|1-e^{i(\psi+\alpha)}|,|1-e^{i(\psi-\alpha)}|\}$. If $\psi\ge0$, put $t=\psi+\alpha\in[\alpha,3\pi/2]$. For $t\le\pi$, $\sin(t/2)\ge\sin(\alpha/2)$ by [F10]; for $t\ge\pi$, sine decreases on $[\pi/2,3\pi/2]$, so $\sin(t/2)\ge\sin(3\pi/4)$. By [F11,F12], $\sin(3\pi/4)=\sin(\pi/4)=1/\sqrt2$, and $\alpha/2\le\pi/4$ gives $\sin(\alpha/2)\le1/\sqrt2$ by [F10]. If $\psi\le0$, apply the same bound to $t=|\psi|+\alpha$ from the second eigenvalue. By [F9,F10], $|1-e^{ix}|=2|\sin(x/2)|$ and these bounds imply $\|I-W\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|I-\mu W\|_{\mathrm{op}}$.

Left multiplication by $R$ preserves operator norm, since it preserves the norm of every vector in the maximum [F3]. As $W=e^{in\pi/8}R^*U$, step 2.1 implies $\|R-e^{in\pi/8}U\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|I-W\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|R-\lambda U\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. Write $n=2q+r$ with $r\in\{0,1\}$. Then $e^{in\pi/8}=\omega^q e^{ir\pi/8}$. Since $\omega^q$ is a free scalar Clifford phase in [F6], moving it between the explicit scalar and the representative leaves the projective T-count unchanged. Thus the two phase representatives are $e^{ir\pi/8}\in\{1,e^{i\pi/8}\}$, proving the reduction.

In the control-first basis [F8], direct block multiplication gives $C(\lambda U)=\operatorname{diag}(I,\lambda U)=(\operatorname{diag}(1,\lambda)\otimes I)C(U)$, in agreement with the supplier identity [F7]. The first factor is generally not a global scalar on the joint control-target system, so replacing $U$ by $\lambda U$ under control requires this relative phase correction.

For nonzero $z\in D$, define
$\operatorname{sde}(z)=\min\{k\in\mathbb Z:(\sqrt2)^kz\in O\}$; exponents may
be negative. Set $\operatorname{sde}(0)=-\infty$. For a matrix $U$, the
denominator statistic used in the synthesis statements below is
$\operatorname{sde}(|U_{00}|^2)$, the exponent of the squared modulus of its
upper-left entry. The base regime in this convention is exponent at most $3$.

For nonzero $z\in D$, write $s=\operatorname{sde}(z)$. There is
$m\in\{0,1\}$ such that
$\operatorname{sde}(|z|^2)=2s-m$. In particular, if
$\operatorname{sde}(|z|^2)\le3$, then $\operatorname{sde}(z)\le2$.

For $x=a+b\omega+c\omega^2+d\omega^3\in O$, multiplication by
$\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ has coefficient vector
$(b-d,a+c,b+d,c-a)$. Consequently $\sqrt2$ divides $x$ in $O$ exactly when
$a\equiv c$ and $b\equiv d\pmod2$. Also,

$$x\bar x=P+\sqrt2Q,\qquad P=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2,\quad Q=a(b-d)+c(b+d),$$

and $2$ divides $x\bar x$ in $O$ exactly when $\sqrt2$ divides $x$.

Let $\bullet$ be the automorphism of $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$ defined in
[[def-qc-cyclotomic-bullet-automorphism]], so $\omega^\bullet=-\omega=\omega^5$,
and let $u\in D\setminus\{0\}$ satisfy
$|u|\le1$ and $|u^\bullet|\le1$. Then $k=\operatorname{sde}(u)\ge0$. If
$a=(\sqrt2)^ku=a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3$, then

$$|a_j|\le2^{k/2}\quad(0\le j\le3).$$

Thus for each fixed $k$ only finitely many coefficient vectors can occur; the
integer search may be restricted to
$|a_j|\le\lfloor2^{k/2}\rfloor$.

Let $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The one-qubit generators and exact matrices in the
ordered computational basis are

$$H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega\end{pmatrix},\qquad T^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$

On basis vectors, $H|q\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^q|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and
$T^k|q\rangle=\omega^{kq}|q\rangle$ for $q\in\{0,1\}$.

Write $S=T^2=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)$ and
$Z=T^4=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. Pauli $X,Y,Z$ are as in
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]]. On two ordered wires,
$\operatorname{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,b\mathbin\oplus a\rangle$; the first wire
is control and the second target. A circuit is a finite chronological word of
these gates at stated wire positions; its matrix is the product with later
gates on the left. No extra wire or controlled-$T$ operation is implicit.

The scalar phase $\omega I$ is an allowed Clifford phase in the one-qubit
matrix-word convention. Its scalar factor is retained in exact matrix products;
the convention that an overall scalar does not affect a resource count is
stated separately from matrix equality. It does not grant a controlled-$T$
operation or allow a scalar on a target wire to be discarded under control.

The exact one-qubit H/T algebra is generated by $H,T,T^\dagger$; $S$ and $Z$
are aliases for the displayed powers. The distinction between exact matrix
equality and [[def-qc-global-phase-equivalence|global-phase equivalence]] is
maintained. Resource costs are supplied by
[[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]] and remain separate from this matrix
definition.

Let $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, where $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The class $[5]_8$ is a
unit modulo $8$, so the cyclotomic Galois group supplier
[[cor-the-galois-group-of-a-rational-cyclotomic-field]] gives the unique
$\mathbb Q$-automorphism $\bullet$ with
$\omega^\bullet=\omega^5=-\omega$. It fixes $i=\omega^2$ and sends
$\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ to $-\sqrt2$. Complex conjugation and $\bullet$
commute, as is checked on the generator $\omega$. The four embeddings of $K$
are the identity, complex conjugation, $\bullet$, and their composite,
because the Galois group consists of the four maps $\omega\mapsto\omega^j$
for $j=1,3,5,7$. Since $\bullet$ fixes $1/2$ and maps $\omega$ into
$\mathbb Z[\omega]$, it preserves $D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$.

This is the nontrivial real-conjugation embedding used in the scaled-grid
conditions; it is distinct from complex conjugation.
If $z\in D$ and $z\bar z=1$, then $z=\omega^j$ for some $j\in\{0,1,\ldots,7\}$.

derivations.claim: For a nonzero real element $P+\sqrt2Q\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$, define $\nu(P+\sqrt2Q)$ as the largest $r\ge0$ for which $(\sqrt2)^r$ divides it in $O$. This maximum exists: divisibility by $(\sqrt2)^{2q}=2^q$ forces both integer coefficients $P,Q$ to be divisible by $2^q$, which cannot hold for arbitrarily large $q$ unless the element is zero. If $y=(\sqrt2)^j y_0$ with $\sqrt2\nmid y_0$, then the definition of sde gives $\operatorname{sde}(y/(\sqrt2)^r)=r-j$.

Applying each embedding of $K$ to $|u|^2+|v|^2=1$ preserves the identity by [F6]; hence every embedding of each entry has modulus at most $1$. Since $s>3$, $u
e0$. If $v=0$, then $|u|^2=1$ and $s=0$, a contradiction, so $v
e0$ as well. Let $r_u=\operatorname{sde}(u)$ and $r_v=\operatorname{sde}(v)$. From [F2] and $s>3$, $r_u\ge2$. More generally, if $\max(r_u,r_v)\ge1$ and the exponents differ, the same argument below gives a contradiction. If $r_u>r_v$, set $x=(\sqrt2)^{r_u}u$ and $y=(\sqrt2)^{r_v}v$. Then $x ar x+2^{r_u-r_v}y ar y=2^{r_u}$; the right side and second term lie in $2O$, so $x ar x\in2O$. Write $x=a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3$. By [F3], $x ar x=P+\sqrt2Q$ with $P=\sum a_j^2$ and $Q=a_0(a_1-a_3)+a_2(a_1+a_3)$. If $P,Q$ are both even, then $a_0+a_2$ and $a_1+a_3$ have equal parity because $P\equiv(a_0+a_2)+(a_1+a_3)\pmod2$, while $Q\equiv(a_0+a_2)(a_1+a_3)\pmod2$ forces both even. Then [F3] gives $\sqrt2\mid x$, contradicting the minimality of $r_u$. Since $x ar x\in2O$ would make both $P,Q$ even in the power basis, this is impossible. If $r_v>r_u$, interchange $u,v$ and use the same calculation with the larger exponent. Thus $r_u=r_v=:r$. Write $x=(\sqrt2)^ru$ and $y=(\sqrt2)^rv$. Their minimal exponents make both primitive with respect to $\sqrt2$. The same parity argument shows $x ar x$ and $y ar y$ are not divisible by $2$, so their divisibility by $\sqrt2$ is either zero or one. Since $r\ge2$, $x ar x+y ar y=2^r$ is divisible by $\sqrt2$; exactly one of the two norms cannot be divisible by $\sqrt2$, since then their sum would not be divisible by it. Hence $
u(x ar x)=
u(y ar y)=j\in\{0,1\}$. Also $r\ge0$ by [F4], since the entries and their $ ullet$-conjugates are all in the unit disk.

The squared-entry identity [F2] gives $s=2r-j$. If $r\ge3$, then $x ar x+y ar y=2^r$, so the integer forms $P(x),Q(x),P(y),Q(y)$ satisfy $P(x)+P(y)\equiv Q(x)+Q(y)\equiv0\pmod8$. For a real element $P+\sqrt2Q$, direct successive division by $\sqrt2$ gives $
u\ge1\iff2\mid P$, $
u\ge2\iff2\mid P,Q$, $
u\ge3\iff4\mid P$ and $2\mid Q$, and $
u\ge4\iff4\mid P,Q$. These tests depend only on the four coefficients modulo $8$ for every requested exponent through $4$. The finite checker enumerates all $4096$ vectors in $(\mathbb Z/8)^4$, groups the $3072$ vectors with $
u=0$ or $1$, and checks all $393216$ compatible residue pairs. For every pair and each $d=1,2,3$, it finds a $k\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ with $
u(|x+\omega^{-k}y|^2)=j+d$; all $1,179,648$ negative-power targets pass. Taking $d=3$ yields $\operatorname{sde}(|(u+\omega^{-k}v)/\sqrt2|^2)=2(r+1)-(j+3)=s-1$. The same code checks the positive-power form as a cross-check.

The only remaining case with $s>3$ is $r=2,j=0$, so $s=4$. Here $x=2u,y=2v$ satisfy $|x|^2+|y|^2=4$. The four embedding bounds and Fourier coefficient formula in [F4] give $|x_i|,|y_i|\le2$. The checker therefore exhausts all integral coefficient vectors in $[-2,2]^4$ for both columns, retains the $256$ normalized pairs with $\nu(|x|^2)=0$, and verifies for each a $k\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ that $\operatorname{sde}(|(x+\omega^{-k}y)/(\sqrt2)^3|^2)=3$. This proves descent at the boundary $s=4$.

Suppose $s\le3$. If $u\ne0$, [F2] gives $\operatorname{sde}(u)\le2$; if $u=0$, its assigned exponent is $-\infty$. If $v=0$, the unit-circle result [F7] gives $u=\omega^j$, so its power-basis coefficients have absolute value at most $1$. If $u=0$, [F7] gives $v=\omega^j$, with the same coefficient bound. In the remaining case both entries are nonzero. The embedding bounds from step 1.2 and [F4] give nonnegative exponents for both. If either exponent is positive, the unequal-exponent contradiction in step 1.2 forces them equal, so both are at most $2$; if neither is positive, both are $0$. Thus [F4] bounds every numerator coefficient by $2$. The exact enumeration in the certificate contains all such columns: it finds $1537$ possible entries and exactly $208$ normalized columns, with squared-entry exponents $-\infty,0,2,3$ occurring $8,8,64,128$ times. Exact breadth-first search from $(1,0)$ using $H,T,T^\dagger$ reaches every one of the $208$ columns; the stored shortest words have maximum length $16$ and the search visits $7660$ states. Every stored word is re-evaluated by exact rational coefficient arithmetic. Therefore the table prepares every base column.

The bounds in step 2.1 and step 2.2 and step 2.3 prove the enumerated finite sets contain every required case, so the checks prove the descent and base assertions rather than sampling them.

finite_smoke.name: mod-8 residue descent
finite_smoke.result: 393216 normalized residue pairs; 1179648 negative-power and 1179648 positive-power targets; 0 failures.
finite_smoke.asserts:
The squared-entry identity [F2] gives $s=2r-j$. If $r\ge3$, then $x ar x+y ar y=2^r$, so the integer forms $P(x),Q(x),P(y),Q(y)$ satisfy $P(x)+P(y)\equiv Q(x)+Q(y)\equiv0\pmod8$. For a real element $P+\sqrt2Q$, direct successive division by $\sqrt2$ gives
$
u\ge1\iff2\mid P$, $
u\ge2\iff2\mid P,Q$, $
u\ge3\iff4\mid P$ and $2\mid Q$, and $
u\ge4\iff4\mid P,Q$. These tests depend only on the four coefficients modulo $8$ for every requested exponent through $4$. The finite checker enumerates all $4096$ vectors in $(\mathbb Z/8)^4$, groups the $3072$ vectors with $
u=0$ or $1$, and checks all $393216$ compatible residue pairs. For every pair and each $d=1,2,3$, it finds a $k\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ with $
u(|x+\omega^{-k}y|^2)=j+d$; all $1,179,648$ negative-power targets pass. Taking $d=3$ yields
$\operatorname{sde}(|(u+\omega^{-k}v)/\sqrt2|^2)=2(r+1)-(j+3)=s-1$.
The same code checks the positive-power form as a cross-check.

finite_smoke.asserts: The only remaining case with $s>3$ is $r=2,j=0$, so $s=4$. Here $x=2u,y=2v$ satisfy $|x|^2+|y|^2=4$. The four embedding bounds and Fourier coefficient formula in [F4] give $|x_i|,|y_i|\le2$. The checker therefore exhausts all integral coefficient vectors in $[-2,2]^4$ for both columns, retains the $256$ normalized pairs with $\nu(|x|^2)=0$, and verifies for each a $k\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ that $\operatorname{sde}(|(x+\omega^{-k}y)/(\sqrt2)^3|^2)=3$. This proves descent at the boundary $s=4$.

finite_smoke.name: base-column synthesis table
finite_smoke.result: 208 columns reached by exact BFS; 7660 states; maximum shortest word 16.
finite_smoke.asserts: Suppose $s\le3$. If $u\ne0$, [F2] gives $\operatorname{sde}(u)\le2$; if $u=0$, its assigned exponent is $-\infty$. If $v=0$, the unit-circle result [F7] gives $u=\omega^j$, so its power-basis coefficients have absolute value at most $1$. If $u=0$, [F7] gives $v=\omega^j$, with the same coefficient bound. In the remaining case both entries are nonzero. The embedding bounds from step 1.2 and [F4] give nonnegative exponents for both. If either exponent is positive, the unequal-exponent contradiction in step 1.2 forces them equal, so both are at most $2$; if neither is positive, both are $0$. Thus [F4] bounds every numerator coefficient by $2$. The exact enumeration in the certificate contains all such columns: it finds $1537$ possible entries and exactly $208$ normalized columns, with squared-entry exponents $-\infty,0,2,3$ occurring $8,8,64,128$ times. Exact breadth-first search from $(1,0)$ using $H,T,T^\dagger$ reaches every one of the $208$ columns; the stored shortest words have maximum length $16$ and the search visits $7660$ states. Every stored word is re-evaluated by exact rational coefficient arithmetic. Therefore the table prepares every base column.

citations.quote:
Let $G$ be the group of exact one-qubit Clifford+T matrix words, and let
$SU(2)=\{U\in U(2):\det U=1\}$. For every $R\in SU(2)$ and every
$\varepsilon>0$, some $W\in G$ satisfies $\det W=1$ and
$\|R-W\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\varepsilon$.

Set $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$, $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$, and
$D=O[1/2]=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$. The relation $\omega^4=-1$ reduces every
element of $O$ to four integer coefficients in the power basis
$1,\omega,\omega^2,\omega^3$. The canonical dyadic encoding of a nonzero
$z\in D$ is

$$z=(a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3)/2^r,$$

where $r\ge0$ is least and, if $r>0$, the four integers are not all even.
Zero is encoded with $r=0$ and all four coefficients zero. Arithmetic is exact:
multiply polynomials, reduce with $\omega^4=-1$, combine denominators, and
remove the common power of $2$ from the coefficients. The integral-basis
supplier [[thm-cyclotomic-ring-of-integers]] and the proof of
[[lem-qc-dyadic-coefficient-encoding]] justify existence and uniqueness.

Let $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The one-qubit generators and exact matrices in the
ordered computational basis are

$$H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega\end{pmatrix},\qquad T^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$

On basis vectors, $H|q\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^q|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and
$T^k|q\rangle=\omega^{kq}|q\rangle$ for $q\in\{0,1\}$.

Write $S=T^2=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)$ and
$Z=T^4=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. Pauli $X,Y,Z$ are as in
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]]. On two ordered wires,
$\operatorname{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,b\mathbin\oplus a\rangle$; the first wire
is control and the second target. A circuit is a finite chronological word of
these gates at stated wire positions; its matrix is the product with later
gates on the left. No extra wire or controlled-$T$ operation is implicit.

The scalar phase $\omega I$ is an allowed Clifford phase in the one-qubit
matrix-word convention. Its scalar factor is retained in exact matrix products;
the convention that an overall scalar does not affect a resource count is
stated separately from matrix equality. It does not grant a controlled-$T$
operation or allow a scalar on a target wire to be discarded under control.

The exact one-qubit H/T algebra is generated by $H,T,T^\dagger$; $S$ and $Z$
are aliases for the displayed powers. The distinction between exact matrix
equality and [[def-qc-global-phase-equivalence|global-phase equivalence]] is
maintained. Resource costs are supplied by
[[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]] and remain separate from this matrix
definition.

Let $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, where $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The class $[5]_8$ is a
unit modulo $8$, so the cyclotomic Galois group supplier
[[cor-the-galois-group-of-a-rational-cyclotomic-field]] gives the unique
$\mathbb Q$-automorphism $\bullet$ with
$\omega^\bullet=\omega^5=-\omega$. It fixes $i=\omega^2$ and sends
$\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ to $-\sqrt2$. Complex conjugation and $\bullet$
commute, as is checked on the generator $\omega$. The four embeddings of $K$
are the identity, complex conjugation, $\bullet$, and their composite,
because the Galois group consists of the four maps $\omega\mapsto\omega^j$
for $j=1,3,5,7$. Since $\bullet$ fixes $1/2$ and maps $\omega$ into
$\mathbb Z[\omega]$, it preserves $D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$.

This is the nontrivial real-conjugation embedding used in the scaled-grid
conditions; it is distinct from complex conjugation.

Let $\theta\in\mathbb R$, $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, and
$$U=\begin{pmatrix}u&-\bar t\\t&\bar u\end{pmatrix}\in SU(2).$$
Then
$$\|R_z(\theta)-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)\ge1-\varepsilon^2/2.$$

derivations.claim: By [F2,F3], the entries of $T,T^\dagger$ lie in $D$. Also $\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ and $1/\sqrt2=(\omega-\omega^3)/2$, so every entry of $H$ lies in $D$. The ring $D$ is closed under complex conjugation because $\bar\omega=\omega^{-1}=\omega^7\in D$. Apply [F1] to $R_z(\theta)\in SU(2)$ and choose an exact word $U$ with $\det U=1$ and $\|R_z(\theta)-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\varepsilon$. Every entry of $U$ lies in $D$ because each generator has entries in $D$ and products of matrices over a subring remain over that subring. Let the first column be $(u,t)^T$. It is a unit vector; its orthogonal unit vector $(-\bar t,\bar u)^T$ is therefore the second column up to a unit scalar $\lambda$. The determinant of the resulting matrix is $\lambda$, so $\det U=1$ forces $\lambda=1$. Hence $U=\begin{pmatrix}u&-\bar t\\t&\bar u\end{pmatrix}$ and $t^\dagger t=1-u^\dagger u$.

Applying $\bullet$ to $U^*U=I$ preserves products and fixes $I$; [F4] also makes it commute with the adjoint. Thus $U^\bullet$ is unitary, and its first-column norm gives $|u^\bullet|^2+|t^\bullet|^2=1$. The original first column similarly gives $|u|^2+|t|^2=1$, so $|u|,|u^\bullet|\le1$.

The strict approximation in step 1.1 and [F5] imply $\operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)>1-\varepsilon^2/2$, hence the required weak inequality. Together with step 1.1 this gives a grid candidate and an exact solution of its norm equation.

citations.quote:
Every finite circuit on $n$ ordered wires using only the matrices in
[[def-qc-clifford-t-gate-library]] has all matrix entries in $D$.

If $U=\begin{pmatrix}u&b\\v&d\end{pmatrix}$ is a $2\times2$ unitary with
entries in $D$, then for some $j\in\{0,\ldots,7\}$,

$$U=\begin{pmatrix}u&-\omega^j\bar v\\v&\omega^j\bar u\end{pmatrix},\qquad |u|^2+|v|^2=1.$$

Let $(u,v)^T$ be a unit vector with entries in $D$, and put
$s=\operatorname{sde}(|u|^2)$. If $s>3$, then some $k\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ has

$$\operatorname{sde}\!\left(\left|\frac{u+\omega^{-k}v}{\sqrt2}\right|^2\right)=s-1.$$

Moreover, every such unit column with $s\le3$ is prepared exactly from
$|0\rangle$ by a word in $H,T,T^\dagger$. A complete coefficient-and-word
table for the finite base set is recorded at
`research/quantum-computing-algorithms-60-2026-10-15-batch-13-finite-certificates.json`.
If $z\in D$ and $z\bar z=1$, then $z=\omega^j$ for some $j\in\{0,1,\ldots,7\}$.

derivations.claim: If $U$ is a finite Clifford+T circuit matrix, [F1] puts all its entries in $D$.

Conversely, let $U\in U(2)$ have entries in $D$. By [F2] its first column $(u,v)^T$ is a normalized column. Apply the descent in [F3] repeatedly while $s=\operatorname{sde}(|u|^2)>3$. Each step replaces the current matrix $M$ by $HT^{-k}M$ and decreases the nonnegative integer $s$ by exactly one; hence after finitely many steps the first column lies in the base regime.

By [F3], the base column has a word $W_0$ with $W_0|0\rangle=(u_0,v_0)^T$. Reversing each descent step by prepending its recorded $T^kH$ gives a word $W$ with first column equal to the original $(u,v)^T$. The unitary $W^*U$ has first column $(1,0)^T$, so orthogonality of its columns makes it $\operatorname{diag}(1,\lambda)$ for a unit scalar $\lambda$. Its entries lie in $D$, since $W,U$ have entries in that ring. Therefore [F4] gives $\lambda=\omega^j$, and $U=WT^j$ is a finite Clifford+T word.
Both implications are proved. The proof constructs the converse word with only exact coefficient operations and the finite base lookup; no approximation, ancilla, or multi-qubit inference is used.

citations.quote:
Use $G=\{H,T,T^\dagger,S,S^\dagger,X,Y,Z\}$ and allow scalar phases $\omega^qI$. Only $H$ contributes to the H count; only $T,T^\dagger$ contribute to the T count. Every word can be rewritten, with its exact scalar retained, as

$$\omega^q T^a H T^{b_1}H\cdots H T^{b_{h-1}}H T^c X^e,$$

where all $b_i$ are odd, exponents are read modulo $8$, and $e\in\{0,1\}$. For $h=0$ interpret this as $\omega^qT^aX^e$. The rewriting never increases either resource count. Each odd power uses one T gate and even powers use none. A reduced word with $h\ge2$ has $\operatorname{sde}(|U_{00}|^2)=h+1$; with $h=1$ the exponent is $2$, and with $h=0$ the squared entry is $0$ or $1$. Consequently reduced words minimize H count among all words for the same matrix up to global phase.

Input a $2\times2$ matrix $U$ as four canonical elements of $D$. Perform the
following exact procedure.

1. Test $U^*U=I$ by rational coefficient arithmetic. If it fails, return
   `INVALID`.
2. Set $M=U$ and an empty list $K$. While
   $s=\operatorname{sde}(|M_{00}|^2)>3$, test $k=0,1,2,3$ in that order and
   choose the first for which
$\operatorname{sde}(|(HT^{-k}M)_{00}|^2)=s-1$. Append $k$ to $K$ and replace
$M$ by $HT^{-k}M$.
3. Look up the first column of $M$ in the complete base-column table at
   `research/quantum-computing-algorithms-60-2026-10-15-batch-13-finite-certificates.json`.
   Let $W_0$ be its stored H/T preparation word. Compute
   $W_0^*M=\operatorname{diag}(1,\lambda)$ exactly and find $j\in\{0,\ldots,7\}$
   with $\lambda=\omega^j$.
4. If $K=(k_1,\ldots,k_r)$ in reduction order, form the exact matrix-word
factorization
$$U=(T^{k_1}H)\cdots(T^{k_r}H)W_0T^j.$$
For the chronological output, emit $T^j$ first, then the stored chronological
gate list for $W_0$, then for $i=r,r-1,\ldots,1$ emit $H$ followed by
$T^{k_i}$. The QC09 semantics put later gates on the left, so this list has the
displayed matrix product.
5. Reduce this word by the exact stack rewriting in
   [[lem-qc-hadamard-reduced-word-denominators]]: move Pauli $X$ factors to
   the right, combine diagonal powers modulo eight, and replace each
   $HT^{2r}H$ by its zero- or one-H Clifford expression until all interior
   diagonal powers are odd. Retain the scalar phase $\omega^qI$ produced by
   these identities in the exact output. Emit even powers as $S,Z$ factors
   and odd powers as one $T$ or $T^\dagger$ with free $S,Z$ factors, then
   return the reduced factors in reverse order as the chronological list.

The denominator descent and table completeness are the mathematical
properties in [[lem-qc-clifford-t-denominator-descent-and-base]] and
[[thm-qc-single-qubit-exact-clifford-t-characterization]]. The finite lookup
table uses exact rational coefficients; no numerical equality tolerance is
used.

Let $(u,v)^T$ be a unit vector with entries in $D$, and put
$s=\operatorname{sde}(|u|^2)$. If $s>3$, then some $k\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ has

$$\operatorname{sde}\!\left(\left|\frac{u+\omega^{-k}v}{\sqrt2}\right|^2\right)=s-1.$$

Moreover, every such unit column with $s\le3$ is prepared exactly from
$|0\rangle$ by a word in $H,T,T^\dagger$. A complete coefficient-and-word
table for the finite base set is recorded at
`research/quantum-computing-algorithms-60-2026-10-15-batch-13-finite-certificates.json`.

Let $\bullet$ be the automorphism of $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$ defined in
[[def-qc-cyclotomic-bullet-automorphism]], so $\omega^\bullet=-\omega=\omega^5$,
and let $u\in D\setminus\{0\}$ satisfy
$|u|\le1$ and $|u^\bullet|\le1$. Then $k=\operatorname{sde}(u)\ge0$. If
$a=(\sqrt2)^ku=a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3$, then

$$|a_j|\le2^{k/2}\quad(0\le j\le3).$$

Thus for each fixed $k$ only finitely many coefficient vectors can occur; the
integer search may be restricted to
$|a_j|\le\lfloor2^{k/2}\rfloor$.

For nonzero $z\in D$, write $s=\operatorname{sde}(z)$. There is
$m\in\{0,1\}$ such that
$\operatorname{sde}(|z|^2)=2s-m$. In particular, if
$\operatorname{sde}(|z|^2)\le3$, then $\operatorname{sde}(z)\le2$.

derivations.claim: By [F2,F3], before the final reduction the compiler has an exact word for $U$. By [F1] its final reduced word is exact and H-optimal, and $n\ge4$ makes its H count $h=n-1$. Write its endpoint exponents $a,c$ and its trailing Pauli factor $X^e$ as in [F1]. Each of the $h-1$ odd interior powers costs one T, so its T count is $h-1+p(a)+p(c)$, where $p(r)=r\bmod2\in\{0,1\}$.

Every Clifford block generated by $H,S,X,Y,Z$ reduces by [F1] to at most one H: all diagonal exponents remain even during that reduction. Splitting any word containing $t$ T gates into $t+1$ Clifford blocks therefore proves $h(V)\le t(V)+1$ for every represented $V$. This argument applies to $T^\dagger$ equally.

There are $n-3$ descent iterations and a constant-size base lookup. Each trial uses boundedly many coefficient additions, sign permutations, multiplications by fixed ring constants, and denominator tests. At every iteration all embeddings of the current unitary remain unitary, so all embedded entries have modulus at most one. For a positive squared-entry exponent, the complementary squared norm has the same exponent: subtracting its primitive numerator from the positive power of $\sqrt2$ leaves it primitive. Thus [F5] bounds every entry exponent by $(n+1)/2$; the base regime is bounded by [F3]. By [F4] all numerator coefficients have $O(n+1)$ bits. Denominator tests need no integer multiplication: for $x=a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3\ne0$, let $m$ be the minimum of the binary trailing-zero counts of its nonzero coefficients, and put $y=x/2^m$. Its $\sqrt2$-valuation is $2m+\delta$, where $\delta=1$ exactly when both opposite-coefficient sums of $y$ are even. Indeed $y$ is not divisible by $2$, so it can contain at most one factor $\sqrt2$. For the resulting primitive numerator $z$, its norm has zero or one factor $\sqrt2$ by [F5]; this factor occurs exactly when $\sum z_i$ is even, since the rational coefficient of $z\bar z$ is $\sum z_i^2$. These parity and trailing-zero scans take $O(n+1)$ bit operations. Every descent trial therefore costs $O(n+1)$ bits and boundedly many ring operations, with coefficient valuations counted as linear binary scans.

Choose $\ell$ and $j$ with $a+\ell$ and $c-j$ odd. Then $HT^\ell UT^jH$ has an odd-interior reduced word with $h+2$ H gates: commute $X^e$ past $T^jH$ using the identities in [F1], which changes only the sign of $j$ and adds a free terminal $Z$ when $e=1$. Its H count is therefore minimal. Conversely if either parity condition fails, the adjacent even-interior pair reduces, giving strictly fewer than $h+2$ H gates. Thus the extension condition is equivalent to $p(\ell)=1-p(a)$ and $p(j)=1-p(c)$.

Apply step 1.2 to the extended matrix $V=HT^\ell UT^jH$. Multiplication by these endpoint factors gives $t(V)\le t(U)+p(\ell)+p(j)$, while $h(V)=h+2$ gives $t(V)\ge h+1$. Consequently $t(U)\ge h+1-p(\ell)-p(j)=h-1+p(a)+p(c)$. Step 1.1 attains this bound, proving simultaneous optimality and both formulas. The same argument proves the endpoint formula for every reduced word with at least one H, since its extension still has at least three H gates and [F1] applies.

The initial word has $O(n+1)$ gates and its stack reduction is linear by [F1], retaining only exponents modulo eight and a scalar exponent modulo eight. The preceding bounds give $O(n+1)$ ring operations and $O((n+1)^2)$ bit operations overall. Any word's total H/T count is at least $h(U)=n-1$; the output has $h+t\le2h+1=O(n+1)$ by step 1.1. Hence $n+1=\Theta(n_{\rm opt}+1)$, proving the claimed bounds.

Extending a reduced h>=1 word by HT^ell and T^jH gives h+2 iff both endpoint parities are complemented; trailing X changes j sign only and adds free Z. This gives the lower bound h−1+p(a)+p(c), attained by the reduced word, including h=1,2. Thus for n>=4 h=n−1 and t=h+1−p(ell)−p(j); the corrected formula in Remarks is consistent with U=HTHTH. Descent uses n−3 iterations and constant base words; all embeddings remain unitary, giving O(n) coefficient bits. Trailing-zero and opposite-coefficient parity tests compute valuations in linear scans, avoiding hidden large multiplication in the descent trials; stack reduction is linear. O(n) ring/O(n²) bit bounds follow and n+1 is comparable to minimal total H/T count. Ordinary canonical input and separate costs retained. No defect found.

citations.quote:
Input a $2\times2$ matrix $U$ as four canonical elements of $D$. Perform the
following exact procedure.

1. Test $U^*U=I$ by rational coefficient arithmetic. If it fails, return
   `INVALID`.
2. Set $M=U$ and an empty list $K$. While
   $s=\operatorname{sde}(|M_{00}|^2)>3$, test $k=0,1,2,3$ in that order and
   choose the first for which
$\operatorname{sde}(|(HT^{-k}M)_{00}|^2)=s-1$. Append $k$ to $K$ and replace
$M$ by $HT^{-k}M$.
3. Look up the first column of $M$ in the complete base-column table at
   `research/quantum-computing-algorithms-60-2026-10-15-batch-13-finite-certificates.json`.
   Let $W_0$ be its stored H/T preparation word. Compute
   $W_0^*M=\operatorname{diag}(1,\lambda)$ exactly and find $j\in\{0,\ldots,7\}$
   with $\lambda=\omega^j$.
4. If $K=(k_1,\ldots,k_r)$ in reduction order, form the exact matrix-word
factorization
$$U=(T^{k_1}H)\cdots(T^{k_r}H)W_0T^j.$$
For the chronological output, emit $T^j$ first, then the stored chronological
gate list for $W_0$, then for $i=r,r-1,\ldots,1$ emit $H$ followed by
$T^{k_i}$. The QC09 semantics put later gates on the left, so this list has the
displayed matrix product.
5. Reduce this word by the exact stack rewriting in
   [[lem-qc-hadamard-reduced-word-denominators]]: move Pauli $X$ factors to
   the right, combine diagonal powers modulo eight, and replace each
   $HT^{2r}H$ by its zero- or one-H Clifford expression until all interior
   diagonal powers are odd. Retain the scalar phase $\omega^qI$ produced by
   these identities in the exact output. Emit even powers as $S,Z$ factors
   and odd powers as one $T$ or $T^\dagger$ with free $S,Z$ factors, then
   return the reduced factors in reverse order as the chronological list.

The denominator descent and table completeness are the mathematical
properties in [[lem-qc-clifford-t-denominator-descent-and-base]] and
[[thm-qc-single-qubit-exact-clifford-t-characterization]]. The finite lookup
table uses exact rational coefficients; no numerical equality tolerance is
used.

Let $(u,v)^T$ be a unit vector with entries in $D$, and put
$s=\operatorname{sde}(|u|^2)$. If $s>3$, then some $k\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ has

$$\operatorname{sde}\!\left(\left|\frac{u+\omega^{-k}v}{\sqrt2}\right|^2\right)=s-1.$$

Moreover, every such unit column with $s\le3$ is prepared exactly from
$|0\rangle$ by a word in $H,T,T^\dagger$. A complete coefficient-and-word
table for the finite base set is recorded at
`research/quantum-computing-algorithms-60-2026-10-15-batch-13-finite-certificates.json`.
If $z\in D$ and $z\bar z=1$, then $z=\omega^j$ for some $j\in\{0,1,\ldots,7\}$.

For nonzero $z\in D$, define
$\operatorname{sde}(z)=\min\{k\in\mathbb Z:(\sqrt2)^kz\in O\}$; exponents may
be negative. Set $\operatorname{sde}(0)=-\infty$. For a matrix $U$, the
denominator statistic used in the synthesis statements below is
$\operatorname{sde}(|U_{00}|^2)$, the exponent of the squared modulus of its
upper-left entry. The base regime in this convention is exponent at most $3$.

Let $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The one-qubit generators and exact matrices in the
ordered computational basis are

$$H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega\end{pmatrix},\qquad T^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$

On basis vectors, $H|q\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^q|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and
$T^k|q\rangle=\omega^{kq}|q\rangle$ for $q\in\{0,1\}$.

Write $S=T^2=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)$ and
$Z=T^4=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. Pauli $X,Y,Z$ are as in
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]]. On two ordered wires,
$\operatorname{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,b\mathbin\oplus a\rangle$; the first wire
is control and the second target. A circuit is a finite chronological word of
these gates at stated wire positions; its matrix is the product with later
gates on the left. No extra wire or controlled-$T$ operation is implicit.

The scalar phase $\omega I$ is an allowed Clifford phase in the one-qubit
matrix-word convention. Its scalar factor is retained in exact matrix products;
the convention that an overall scalar does not affect a resource count is
stated separately from matrix equality. It does not grant a controlled-$T$
operation or allow a scalar on a target wire to be discarded under control.

The exact one-qubit H/T algebra is generated by $H,T,T^\dagger$; $S$ and $Z$
are aliases for the displayed powers. The distinction between exact matrix
equality and [[def-qc-global-phase-equivalence|global-phase equivalence]] is
maintained. Resource costs are supplied by
[[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]] and remain separate from this matrix
definition.

For a gate occurrence $g=(\gamma,w)$ in a circuit on $\mathcal Q_n$, let $\widetilde U_g$ be the global embedding from [[lem-qc-local-gate-wire-embedding]]. For a layer $L_t=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$, define
$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$
For a circuit with chronological layers $L_1,\ldots,L_d$, define
$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

Use $G=\{H,T,T^\dagger,S,S^\dagger,X,Y,Z\}$ and allow scalar phases $\omega^qI$. Only $H$ contributes to the H count; only $T,T^\dagger$ contribute to the T count. Every word can be rewritten, with its exact scalar retained, as

$$\omega^q T^a H T^{b_1}H\cdots H T^{b_{h-1}}H T^c X^e,$$

where all $b_i$ are odd, exponents are read modulo $8$, and $e\in\{0,1\}$. For $h=0$ interpret this as $\omega^qT^aX^e$. The rewriting never increases either resource count. Each odd power uses one T gate and even powers use none. A reduced word with $h\ge2$ has $\operatorname{sde}(|U_{00}|^2)=h+1$; with $h=1$ the exponent is $2$, and with $h=0$ the squared entry is $0$ or $1$. Consequently reduced words minimize H count among all words for the same matrix up to global phase.

derivations.claim: Initially $U=I\cdot M$ with $M=U$. If a loop iteration records $k$ and sets $M'=HT^{-k}M$, then $M=T^kHM'$. Therefore, after $r$ reductions, the recorded sequence $K=(k_1,\ldots,k_r)$ satisfies $U=(T^{k_1}H)\cdots(T^{k_r}H)M$.

At every iteration, $M$ remains unitary with entries in $D$, since the matrices in [F5] are unitary over $D$. If its exponent exceeds $3$, [F2] ensures that the finite search over $k=0,1,2,3$ finds a value reducing that integer exponent by exactly one. Thus the loop terminates after finitely many iterations with exponent at most $3$.

Let $W_0$ be the table word for the first column of the terminal $M$. Then $W_0^*M$ is unitary with first column $(1,0)^T$, hence is $\operatorname{diag}(1,\lambda)$ for a unit scalar $\lambda$. Its entries lie in $D$, so [F3] gives $\lambda=\omega^j$ for some $j\in\{0,\ldots,7\}$. Consequently $M=W_0T^j$.

Substituting this identity into step 1.1 yields exactly the matrix factorization returned in [F1]. The algorithm emits its factors from right to left as a chronological gate list; [F6] says later gates multiply on the left, so that list has the displayed matrix. The final reduction preserves this matrix by [F7], including its scalar factor. Hence the returned word implements $U$ exactly.
