Put $R=\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$, $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$, and
$\lambda=1+\sqrt2$. Both rings are norm-Euclidean domains and hence unique
factorization domains with effective gcd and associate tests. There is a
terminating finite-search algorithm factoring every nonzero element of $O$
into primes and a unit. The units of $R$ are exactly $\pm\lambda^j$
($j\in\mathbb Z$); a unit is positive at both real embeddings if and only
if it is a square of a unit of $R$. These assertions include effective square
root recovery. No polynomial runtime bound is asserted for finite-search
factorization.

For every $\xi\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2,1/2]$ there is a terminating exact
algorithm deciding whether $t^\dagger t=\xi$ has a solution
$t\in D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$, and returning such a solution when one
exists. A supplied prime factorization of the numerator of
$\xi^\bullet\xi$ is permissible but unnecessary for the finite-search
version below. No polynomial runtime bound is asserted.

More explicitly, reject a negative real embedding; handle $\xi=0$ by
$t=0$. Otherwise choose $r\ge0$ with $\eta=4^r\xi\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$
and factor $\eta$ into primes of $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$. Group the prime
associate classes into orbits of complex conjugation. There is a solution
exactly when every conjugation-fixed class has even exponent. The
conjugation-paired classes have equal exponents automatically. Allocate half
of each fixed exponent, and the whole exponent to one representative of each
pair, to form $s$. Recover a real unit $v$ with
$v^2=\eta/(s^\dagger s)$; then $t=vs/2^r$ is an exact solution.

Given a prime integer $p$ and an integer $a$, there is an exact randomized algorithm that returns a square root of $a$ modulo $p$ or correctly reports that none exists. With ordinary binary integers, schoolbook arithmetic and independent unbiased random bits, its expected bit cost is polynomial in the input length; after reducing $a$ modulo $p$, it is $O((1+\log p)^4)$. Every returned answer is correct, and the algorithm terminates with probability one. The input promise that $p$ is prime is not a primality test.

For every odd prime $p$,

$$\left(\frac{-1}{p}\right)=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}.$$

Equivalently, $(-1/p)=1$ if and only if $p\equiv1\pmod4$, while $(-1/p)=-1$ if and only if $p\equiv3\pmod4$.

For every odd prime $p$,

$$\left(\frac2p\right)=(-1)^{(p^2-1)/8}.$$

Equivalently, $(2/p)=1$ if and only if $p\equiv1$ or $7\pmod8$, while $(2/p)=-1$ if and only if $p\equiv3$ or $5\pmod8$.

For every odd prime $p$ and all integers $a,b$,

$$\left(\frac{ab}{p}\right)=\left(\frac ap\right)\left(\frac bp\right).$$

Consequently, if $p\nmid c$, then $(ac^2/p)=(a/p)$.

For every prime $p$, the operations of addition and multiplication on
$\mathbb Z/p$ make it a field ([[def-field]]).

derivations.claim: Reject if either real embedding of $\xi$ is negative, and return zero if $\xi=0$. Signs of $a+b\sqrt2$ are determined by coefficient signs and comparison of $a^2$ with $2b^2$, so these are exact polynomial bit operations. A zero real embedding implies $\xi=0$ by injectivity. Otherwise both embeddings are positive. Clear a rational square denominator by choosing the least $r\ge0$ with $\eta=4^r\xi\in R$. Since the input uses explicit denominators, $r=O(L)$ and $\eta$ has $O(L)$-bit coefficients. Its positive rational norm is $N_R(\eta)=2^{4r-\ell}n$, so its factorization is obtained from the supplied one by adjoining the known factor $2$. All its prime factors and their multiplicities have total size polynomial in $L$.

Here are polynomial bit gcd and associate procedures for [F1], with coefficient growth controlled. Use $N_R(a+b\sqrt2)=|a^2-2b^2|$ and $N_O(z)=|z|^2|z^\bullet|^2$. The real coefficient-rounding error has norm at most $1/2$. Write the cyclotomic rounding error as $C+D\omega$, where $C=x+iy$, $D=z+it$ and $|x|,|y|,|z|,|t|\le1/2$. Put $S=|C|^2+|D|^2$. If $S\le9/10$, then $N_O(C+D\omega)=|C^2-iD^2|^2\le S^2\le81/100$. If $S>9/10$, each of the four squared real coordinates exceeds $3/20$, since the other three sum to at most $3/4$. Thus $|\operatorname{Re}C^2|,|\operatorname{Re}D^2|<1/10$ and $|\operatorname{Im}C^2|,|\operatorname{Im}D^2|\le1/2$. Expanding the square gives $|C^2-iD^2|^2\le |C|^4+|D|^4+2(|\operatorname{Re}C^2||\operatorname{Im}D^2|+|\operatorname{Im}C^2||\operatorname{Re}D^2|)\le1/2+1/5=7/10$. Hence every cyclotomic remainder contracts the norm by at most $\rho=81/100$. As $(81/100)^4<1/2$, every four nonzero divisions halve the norm. This explicit estimate needs no compactness premise.

Before and after each division, balance any nonzero remainder $z$ by multiplying it by a power of $\lambda$, which changes neither its norm nor the generated principal ideal. In $R$ arrange $\sqrt{N_R(z)}\le|z|<\lambda\sqrt{N_R(z)}$; in $O$ arrange $N_O(z)^{1/4}\le|z|<\lambda N_O(z)^{1/4}$. The other embedding then has comparable magnitude, since their absolute product is respectively $N_R(z)$ or $\sqrt{N_O(z)}$. The fixed inverse linear conversion from embeddings to power-basis coordinates bounds every balanced coefficient by a constant times $N_R(z)^{1/2}$ or $N_O(z)^{1/4}$. All comparisons can be performed without numerical approximations by squaring and comparing elements of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$. For inputs with $B$-bit coordinates, the initial norm has $O(B)$ bits, and its nonzero conjugates are bounded above by $2^{O(B)}$ and below by $2^{-O(B)}$ using their integer product. Hence initial balancing uses $O(B)$ unit multiplications. Thereafter all balanced coordinates and each exact quotient have $O(B)$ bits; division in the fixed-degree number field uses a fixed number of rational operations. Rounding produces $O(B)$-bit remainders, whose balancing again uses $O(B)$ multiplications. Step 2.1 bounds the number of divisions by $O(B)$. This proves polynomial bit cost for gcds; exact quotient and associate tests have polynomial cost as well. Units used in balancing do not affect any gcd ideal.

Recover all $R$-prime classes above each odd rational prime $p$ in step 1.1 as follows. If $p\equiv3,5\pmod8$, the polynomial $X^2-2$ has no root by [F3], so $R/(p)=\mathbb F_p[X]/(X^2-2)$ is a field by [F4], and $p$ is already prime in $R$. If $p\equiv1,7\pmod8$, compute $b^2=2\pmod p$ using [F3]. Evaluation at the two distinct roots $b,-b$ identifies $R/(p)$ with $\mathbb F_p\times\mathbb F_p$: interpolation of a linear polynomial gives the inverse, since $2b$ is invertible. The gcds $\pi_+=\gcd_R(p,\sqrt2-b)$ and $\pi_-=\gcd_R(p,\sqrt2+b)$ generate the preimages of the two component kernels. Their quotients are fields, so these gcds are nonassociate primes, and the component description shows $(\pi_+\pi_-)=(p)$. These procedures give every $R$-prime over $p$ and use the modular-root algorithm and polynomial gcds of step 3.1.

For an odd $p$ and an $R$-prime $\pi$ just obtained, put $E=R/(\pi)$. Because $2$ is invertible modulo $\pi$ and $\omega=(\sqrt2/2)(1+i)$, there is an explicit isomorphism $O/(\pi)=E[i]=E[T]/(T^2+1)$: the displayed formula expresses $\omega$ in the right-hand ring, and $i=\omega^2$ expresses its inverse map. If $p\equiv7\pmod8$, then $E=\mathbb F_p$ and $T^2+1$ is irreducible by [F3]. Thus $O/(\pi)$ is a field, and $\pi$ is prime also in $O$; its class is fixed by conjugation because $\pi$ is real. If $p\equiv1,5\pmod8$, compute $b^2=-1\pmod p$ and put $h=b+i$. If $p\equiv3\pmod8$, compute $b^2=-2\pmod p$ and put $h=b+i\sqrt2$; the root exists since both characters of $-1$ and $2$ are $-1$ by [F3]. In these cases $T^2+1$ splits into distinct roots in $E$: they are $\pm b$ in the first case and $\pm b/\sqrt2$ in the second. Hence $O/(\pi)$ is a product of two fields, by the same explicit interpolation as in step 4.1. The ideals generated by $(\pi,h)$ and $(\pi,h^\dagger)$ select the two distinct component kernels. Consequently $t=\gcd_O(\pi,h)$ and $t^\dagger$ are nonassociate primes, with $\pi\sim t^\dagger t$. This proves prime recovery and its completeness, rather than merely asserting a splitting table.

Include $\delta$ as the sole prime class over $2$ by [F2]. Step 4.1 and step 5.1 now give a finite list of all $O$-prime classes over the rational prime divisors of $N_R(\eta)$. Every prime of $O$ dividing $\eta$ appears: it divides the integer $\eta\eta^\bullet$, and the prime-divisor property of [F1] makes it divide one of those rational primes. Repeated exact division of $\eta$ by the displayed generators, with associate tests to remove duplicate classes, therefore gives its full prime-class exponent list. The remaining quotient has norm one and is a unit, since otherwise unique factorization would supply a missing prime divisor. Compute conjugation orbits by conjugating the generators and testing associates. Reject exactly when a fixed class has odd exponent; otherwise form $s$ by the allocation in [F2]. This decision and allocation are complete, including the ramified class and arbitrary multiplicities, by [F2].

Put $e=\eta/(s^\dagger s)$. By [F2], this is a real unit of $R$, positive at both embeddings; [F1] gives $e=\lambda^{2j}$ for an integer $j$. Recover its exponent by multiplying $e$ by $\lambda^{-1}$ while it is at least $\lambda$, or by $\lambda$ while it is below $1$, recording the signed number of multiplications. The resulting unit in $[1,\lambda)$ is $1$ by [F1], so this finds $2j$ exactly, including negative exponents. Set $v=\lambda^j$ and return $t=vs/2^r$. Then $t^\dagger t=v^2s^\dagger s/4^r=\xi$. This also states the actual unit-recovery algorithm; no search over arbitrary coefficients is used.

All rational primes in step 1.1 have $O(L)$ bits, and their multiplicities sum to $O(L)$ since their product is an $O(L)$-bit integer. Each gcd in step 4.1 and step 5.1 is normalized as in step 3.1, so its output has $O(L)$-bit coefficients. The number of prime generators is at most four per rational prime. A prime in $O$ has integer norm at least two; consequently step 6.1 uses $O(L)$ successful divisions. Products and quotients of at most $O(L)$ such factors have at most $O(L^2)$ coefficient bits: a product in fixed degree adds operand bit lengths plus a constant, and a field inverse is given by the product of the other conjugates divided by the integer norm. Thus $s$, $e$ and the intermediate divisions have polynomial bit length. An element $\lambda^j$ with $B$-bit coefficients has $|j|=O(B)$, because its two real absolute embeddings are $\lambda^j$ and $\lambda^{-j}$ and both are bounded by $2^{O(B)}$. Step 7.1 therefore takes polynomially many bit operations and produces a polynomial-size answer. Modular-root calls are the only randomized operations; their number is $O(L)$ and each has expected polynomial cost by [F3]. This proves the full expected polynomial bit bound, without using the exhaustive factor search in [F1].

For the bounded case, put $\alpha=(\sqrt2)^k\xi=A+B\sqrt2\in R$. Both absolute embeddings of $\alpha$ are at most $2^{k/2}$, so $|A|\le2^{k/2}$ and $|B|\le2^{k/2}/\sqrt2$. If $k$ is even, $\xi=(A+B\sqrt2)/2^{k/2}$; if $k$ is odd, $\xi=(2B+A\sqrt2)/2^{(k+1)/2}$. These expressions and their reductions have $O(k+1)$ coefficient bits. Moreover $|N_R(\alpha)|=2^k\xi\xi^\bullet\le2^k$ is an integer, so the reduced nonzero numerator $n$ is at most $2^k$ (and hence at most $4^k$); its supplied prime factorization has polynomial length in $k+1$. Thus $L$ is polynomial in $k+1$, and step 8.1 yields the asserted bounded-input complexity. For the candidate case, write $u=z/(\sqrt2)^h$ with $z\in O$. Then $(\sqrt2)^{2h}\xi=2^h-z^\dagger z$ is a real element of $O$, hence lies in $R$ by [F1]; the least residual exponent is at most $2h$. Applying the preceding bounds with that exponent proves $n\le4^h$ and expected polynomial cost in $h+1$. Zero was already handled in step 1.1. For unrestricted inputs, real units can have norm one but arbitrarily large coefficients; retaining $L$ in the general statement is therefore necessary.

We calibrate the last bound for $H=h+1\ge1$. The bounded residual lies in $2^{-h}R$, so write $\xi=(a+b\sqrt2)/2^h$ with $|a|,|b|\le2^h$, by adding and subtracting its two embeddings. Using the least clearing exponent of step 1.1 gives $r\le\lceil h/2\rceil$ and $\eta$-coefficient bit lengths at most $h+2$. The input coefficient denominators divide $2^h$. For prime $n=p$, $p\le2^{2h}$; hence its bit length is at most $2h+1$. The cases $n=0,1$ omit these prime calls. At most two real primes and four cyclotomic primes over $p$, together with $\delta$, need be represented. Reusing the modular roots, at most eight modular-root calls and sixteen ring gcds cover step 4.1 and step 5.1, including harmless duplicate computations. All gcd inputs have coefficient bit lengths at most $8H$: the modular roots are reduced below $p$, and a balanced real factor has coefficients at most $2\sqrt{N_R(p)}=2p$, so converting it to the cyclotomic basis still fits this bound. The real and cyclotomic norm bounds for an integer element with $b$-bit coordinates are respectively $2^{2b+2}$ and $2^{4b+8}$, because each complex embedding has magnitude at most $4\cdot2^b$. Step 2.1 therefore requires fewer than $32(b+2)$ divisions per gcd.

Here is explicit storage and loop bookkeeping for these gcds. Multiplication in the power basis of $O$ has at most four signed product terms per output coefficient, so multiplying elements with coefficient bit lengths $b_1,b_2$ gives lengths at most $b_1+b_2+3$; the real basis obeys the same bound. The other field conjugates only permute or negate coordinates. Forming $x/y$ by multiplying $x$ by the other three conjugates of $y$ and dividing by $N_O(y)$ gives numerator and denominator lengths at most $b_x+3b_y+12$ and $4b_y+12$. Balanced gcd operands have lengths at most $b+6$, by the embedding bounds in step 3.1 and the preceding norm estimate. Thus the unbalanced integer remainder has lengths below $8(b+8)$. Its nonzero embeddings lie between $2^{-8(b+8)-2}$ and $2^{8(b+8)+2}$, by the integer norm and the upper bound for the other embedding. Since $\lambda>2$, balancing needs fewer than $32(b+8)$ unit multiplications, including comparisons; during balancing each embedding stays between its initial and final values, so all coefficient lengths stay below $16(b+8)$. The quotient formulas keep temporary rational coordinates below $512(b+8)$ bits. Allowing eight fixed-degree field actions per balancing iteration and $256$ for division, norm and rounding, $32(b+2)$ divisions, and initial balancing, fewer than $2^{21}(b+8)^2$ field actions suffice per gcd. Here an action means a fixed-degree field multiplication, quotient, norm, sign comparison or coordinate rounding, with their integer-operation costs expanded below.

For the remaining work, the number of prime factors of $\eta$ counted with multiplicity is at most $\log_2N_O(\eta)\le4h+8\le16H$. Balanced prime-generator coefficients have at most $32H$ bits, including $\delta$. Multiplying at most $16H$ generators gives coefficient lengths below $2^{10}H^2$; successive exact divisions increase length by at most $3(32H)+12$ each by step 11.1, hence stay below $2^{12}H^2$. The quotient $e=\eta/(s^\dagger s)$ has length below $2^{14}H^2$. If $e=\lambda^m$, its two embedding bounds and $\lambda>2$ give $|m|<2^{15}H^2$, so both exponent recovery and construction of $\lambda^{m/2}$ use fewer than $2^{16}H^2$ unit multiplications in total. A unit multiplication increases length by at most three; monotonicity of the embedding sizes during exponent reduction, or the direct power formula during reconstruction, bounds every stored coordinate, including the returned numerator and denominator, by $B=2^{20}H^2$ bits. Sixteen gcds with $b\le8H$, at most $16H$ successful divisions and at most one failed division per generator, at most $25$ associate comparisons, and these unit loops, are together fewer than $2^{40}H^4$ field actions; this also includes reading, denominator clearing, allocation, and checking $t^\dagger t=\xi$ exactly before returning. A field action can be implemented using fewer than $4096$ signed integer operations and rational reductions on values of at most $4096(B+1)$ bits: expand the at most four coordinates, the at most three conjugate factors for inversion, and reduce each rational coordinate by the ordinary integer gcd. Binary schoolbook addition, multiplication and long division of $d$-bit integers take fewer than $2^{10}(d+1)^2$ bit steps, by their nested digit loops. An integer gcd has at most $2d+2$ divisions, since every two Euclidean divisions at least halve its positive divisor. For $d\le4096(B+1)$, $4096$ such integer-gcd costs are below $2^{63}(B+1)^3$. Maintaining the at most four binary array-index counters costs at most $64(B+1)$ further bit operations per digit action, since their lengths are at most $13+\lceil\log_2(B+1)\rceil\le16(B+1)$. Including this overhead and the rational reductions, one field action therefore costs less than $2^{70}(B+1)^4$ bit steps. These bounds deliberately allow more integer operations and bits than any of the displayed fixed-degree formulas require.

Finally, for a modular-root call with prime bit length $d$, the sampling implementation of [F3] uses an expected at most eight raw bit strings before finding a nonsquare: sampling accepts with probability at least $1/4$, and half its accepted residues are nonsquares. Binary powering uses at most $2d$ modular multiplications, and the at most $d$ order-reduction iterations use at most $4d$ modular multiplications each. The schoolbook bounds in step 12.1 consequently put the expected cost of one call below $2^{20}(d+1)^5$ bit steps, including sampling and initialization. Since $d\le2H$, eight calls cost less than $2^{31}H^5$ in expectation. The deterministic part is less than $2^{40}H^4\,2^{70}(2^{20}H^2+1)^4\le2^{194}H^{12}$. Adding the random part gives a bound below $2^{195}H^{12}\le2^{200}H^{20}=P(h)$. For $n=0,1$ the omitted prime calls only reduce the bound. This proves the explicit majorant for the actual chosen arithmetic loops, with no timing assumption about composite inputs.

Let $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, where $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The class $[5]_8$ is a
unit modulo $8$, so the cyclotomic Galois group supplier
[[cor-the-galois-group-of-a-rational-cyclotomic-field]] gives the unique
$\mathbb Q$-automorphism $\bullet$ with
$\omega^\bullet=\omega^5=-\omega$. It fixes $i=\omega^2$ and sends
$\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ to $-\sqrt2$. Complex conjugation and $\bullet$
commute, as is checked on the generator $\omega$. The four embeddings of $K$
are the identity, complex conjugation, $\bullet$, and their composite,
because the Galois group consists of the four maps $\omega\mapsto\omega^j$
for $j=1,3,5,7$. Since $\bullet$ fixes $1/2$ and maps $\omega$ into
$\mathbb Z[\omega]$, it preserves $D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$.

This is the nontrivial real-conjugation embedding used in the scaled-grid
conditions; it is distinct from complex conjugation.

Identify $\mathbb{Z}$ with its canonical copy inside $\mathbb{R}$, along the
embeddings $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{R}$
([[lem-nat-embeds-int]], [[lem-int-embeds-rat]], [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]],
[[def-integers]]). Then for every real $x$ there is **exactly one** integer $m$
with

$$m \;\le\; x \;<\; m + 1 .$$

It is written $\lfloor x \rfloor$ and called the **integer part**, or **floor**,
of $x$.

**Two independent ingredients are needed and neither may be dropped.** Existence
is the Archimedean property ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) together with the
well-ordering of $\mathbb{N}$ ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]): the first says
that $x$ is caught between two integers at all, the second picks the *least*
integer above $x$. Uniqueness is the discreteness of $\mathbb{Z}$: no integer
lies strictly between $m$ and $m+1$.

This lemma is stated once here and reused. It is what turns "the nearest integer
to $x$" from a picture into an object, and the companion page's oscillator
$\psi(x) = \inf_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} |x - n|$ is computed from it in one line.

derivations.claim: First suppose $I=[x_0,x_1]$, $J=[y_0,y_1]$ have positive lengths $\delta,\Delta$. Multiplication by the unit $\lambda^r$ on the first embedding and by $(-\lambda^{-1})^r$ on the second is a bijection of the grid solutions. Choose the integer $r$ so the new first length lies in $[\lambda^{-1},1)$, reversing the second interval's endpoints when necessary. This is done by taking an integer part of a logarithm and checking the endpoint inequalities; $P$ is unchanged. Work henceforth with the rescaled intervals. Every solution $a+b\sqrt2$ satisfies $(x_0-y_1)/(2\sqrt2)\le b\le(x_1-y_0)/(2\sqrt2)$. Enumerate the integers in this interval. For each $b$, the interval $[x_0-b\sqrt2,x_1-b\sqrt2]$ has length less than one, so its least integer is the only possible $a$; retain it only if both grid inequalities hold. No solution is duplicated or missed. The number of $b$ proposals is at most $1+(\delta+\Delta)/(2\sqrt2)=O(1+P)$ because $\lambda^{-1}\le\delta<1$ and $\Delta=P/\delta$. The integer endpoints and the affine formula for $b$ give random access to proposals.

Any pair of intervals whose length product is at least $\lambda^3$ contains a solution. Indeed, rescale as above, this time putting the first length in $[\lambda,\lambda^2)$; the second length is then greater than or equal to $\lambda$. For the two interval centers $x,y$, round $(x+y)/2$ and $(x-y)/(2\sqrt2)$ to their nearest integers $a,b$. Both errors $|a+b\sqrt2-x|$ and $|a-b\sqrt2-y|$ are at most $(1+\sqrt2)/2=\lambda/2$, so the rounded point satisfies both constraints. If $P\ge4\lambda^3$, put $q=\lfloor P/(2\lambda^3)\rfloor$. Divide $I$ into $q$ equal cells and use the concentric closed half of each cell. Each resulting interval paired with $J$ has length product $P/(2q)\ge\lambda^3$. Their disjointness gives $q$ distinct solutions, and $q\ge P/(4\lambda^3)$. Consequently the proposal bound in step 1.1 is $O(N+1)$, including the case $P<4\lambda^3$.

If $I$ is a singleton and $J$ has length $\Delta$, replace $I$ temporarily by the concentric interval of length $1/(\Delta+1)$ and test the original equality when filtering proposals. The product is at most one, so step 1.1 gives only constantly many proposals and contains all original solutions. Treat a singleton $J$ symmetrically; if both are singletons, enlarge both to length $1/2$. Empty intervals need no work. For all cases, restore the inverse unit scaling on retained points. Thus the asserted finite list and counting estimates hold without an unbounded search for a witness or a free floor oracle.

derivations.claim: Put $\lambda=1+\sqrt2$ and define $R=\frac1{\sqrt2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&-2\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $B=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&\sqrt2\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $K=\frac1{\sqrt2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-\lambda^{-1}&-1\\\lambda&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $X=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$, and $L=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda,\lambda^{-1})$. Express a determinant-one positive matrix as $D=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}e\lambda^{-z}&b\\b&e\lambda^z\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $e=\sqrt{1+b^2}$; use $\beta,f,\zeta$ for $\Delta$. Define skew $S=b^2+\beta^2$ and bias $\zeta-z$. For a matrix $T$, act on the pair by $(T^{\mathsf T}DT,(T^\bullet)^{\mathsf T}\Delta T^\bullet)$. In real/imaginary coordinates, with $s=1/\sqrt2$, the additive group $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$ is $\{(a+sb,c+sd):a,b,c,d\in\mathbb Z,\ b\equiv d\pmod2\}$. For integer matrices $P,Q$, the real matrix $M=P+sQ$ maps $O$ into $O$ exactly when the sum of the four entries of $P$ is even and all four entries of $Q$ have the same parity; applying $M$ to $(1,0),(0,1),(s,s),(-s,s)$ gives these conditions. In the order (sum parity of $P$, common parity of $Q$, determinant), each of $R,R^{-1}$ has (even, odd, $1$); each of $A,A^{-1}$ has (even, even, $1$); each of $B,B^{-1}$ has (even, even, $1$); each of $K,K^{-1}$ has (even, odd, $1$); $X$ has (even, even, $-1$); $Z$ has (even, even, $-1$); and each of $L,L^{-1}$ has (even, even, $1$). Thus these matrices preserve $O$ and have the stated determinants. Their entries lie in $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$, so [F1] gives the conjugation identity.

The extra maps in the shifted-map factorization also preserve the lattice, including their inverses. With the criterion of step 1.1, $U=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda,1)$, $U^{-1}$, $\lambda I$, and $\lambda^{-1}I$ each have even total integer part and even entries in their $s$-coefficient matrix; hence all four map $O$ into itself. Applying the same criterion to each inverse gives equality with $O$.

A skew-preserving temporary shift replaces $(z,\zeta,b,\beta)$ by $(z-q,\zeta+q,b,(-1)^q\beta)$, where $q=\lfloor(1-(\zeta-z))/2\rfloor$. It puts the bias in $[-1,1]$. This is conjugation by $\sigma^q=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda^{q/2},\lambda^{-q/2})$ on $D$ and by $\tau^q=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda^{-q/2},(-1)^q\lambda^{q/2})$ on $\Delta$. If a lattice map $T$ reduces the shifted pair, then $T'=\sigma^qT\sigma^q$ reduces the original skew by the same factor: shifting again preserves skew and gives precisely the action of $T'$, whose bullet is $(-\tau)^qT^\bullet\tau^q$. This $T'$ is still a lattice map. For $q=1$, its entries are $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\lambda t_{11}&t_{12}\\t_{21}&\lambda^{-1}t_{22}\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, the product $\lambda^{-1}I\operatorname{diag}(\lambda,1)T\operatorname{diag}(\lambda,1)$ of lattice maps; the same argument applies to inverse shifts. Finally apply $Z$ if necessary to make $\beta\ge0$, and $X$ if necessary to make $z+\zeta\ge0$. These preserve skew and the bias strip.

Assume $S\ge15$ and the normalization of step 3.1. In the central region $|z|,|\zeta|\le4/5$, use $R$. Its new off-diagonals are $e\sinh_\lambda z,f\sinh_\lambda\zeta$, where $\sinh_\lambda x=(\lambda^x-\lambda^{-x})/2$. Thus $S'\le S(17/15)\sinh_\lambda^2(4/5)<(9/10)S$. For an explicit strict bound, $\lambda^{4/5}<21/10$ follows from $\lambda<5/2$ and $(5/2)^4<(21/10)^5$, so $\sinh_\lambda(4/5)<341/420$ and $(17/15)(341/420)^2<9/10$.

If $b\ge0$, $z\le3/10$, and $\zeta\ge4/5$, use $K$. Its off-diagonal squares sum to $(\sqrt2 b-e\cosh_\lambda(z+1))^2+(\sqrt2\beta-f\cosh_\lambda(\zeta-1))^2$. Both arguments belong to $[-1/5,13/10]$. For $c=\cosh_\lambda x=(\lambda^x+\lambda^{-x})/2$, the inequality $be\ge b^2$ gives $(\sqrt2 b-ec)^2\le b^2(\sqrt2-c)^2+c^2$, and likewise for $\beta$. On this interval $1\le c<109/60<2\sqrt2-1$, so $(\sqrt2-c)^2\le(\sqrt2-1)^2$. Here the rational bound follows from $\lambda<17/7$, $\lambda^{1/5}<6/5$, $\lambda^{1/10}<11/10$, and $\lambda^{13/10}>12/5$: hence $c<((17/7)(6/5)(11/10)+5/12)/2<109/60$. All fractional-power comparisons follow by raising positive sides to powers five or ten. Therefore $S'/S\le(\sqrt2-1)^2+(2/15)(109/60)^2<9/10$. For $z\ge4/5$, $\zeta\le3/10$, use $K^\bullet$ and exchange the two matrices.

If $b\ge0$ and $z,\zeta\ge3/10$, put $c=\min(z,\zeta)$, $n=\max(1,\lfloor\lambda^c/2\rfloor)$ and use $A^n$. The new off-diagonals are $b-2ne\lambda^{-z}$ and $\beta-2nf\lambda^{-\zeta}$. Expanding their squares and using $be\ge b^2$, $\beta f\ge\beta^2$ gives $S'/S\le\max_{x\in\{z,\zeta\}}(1-2n\lambda^{-x})^2+(8/15)n^2\lambda^{-2c}$. If $\lfloor\lambda^c/2\rfloor\ge1$, then $\lambda^c/4\le n\le\lambda^c/2$ and $c\le z,\zeta\le c+1$; the displayed bound is at most $(1-1/(2\lambda))^2+2/15<9/10$. Otherwise $n=1$, $\lambda^c<2$, and the two arguments $\lambda^{-x}$ lie in $[1/(2\lambda),\lambda^{-3/10}]$. The quadratic's maximum is at the left endpoint: $\lambda^{3/10}>13/10$ and $\lambda>12/5$ verify the endpoint comparison. The bound is then at most $(1-1/\lambda)^2+(8/15)\lambda^{-3/5}<(3/5)^2+8/15<9/10$.

If $b\le0$ and $z,\zeta\ge-1/5$, put $c=\min(z,\zeta)$, $n=\max(1,\lfloor\lambda^c/\sqrt2\rfloor)$ and use $B^n$. Its off-diagonals are $b+\sqrt2ne\lambda^{-z}$ and $\beta-\sqrt2nf\lambda^{-\zeta}$. Since $be\le-b^2$ and $\beta f\ge\beta^2$, expansion gives $S'/S\le\max_{x\in\{z,\zeta\}}(1-\sqrt2 n\lambda^{-x})^2+(4/15)n^2\lambda^{-2c}$. When the floor is positive, $\lambda^c/(2\sqrt2)\le n\le\lambda^c/\sqrt2$, giving at most $(1-1/(2\lambda))^2+2/15<9/10$. Otherwise $n=1$ and $\lambda^{-x}\in[1/(\sqrt2\lambda),\lambda^{1/5}]$. The absolute value at both endpoints is less than $5/7$: use $1-1/\lambda<3/5$, $\sqrt2<10/7$, and $\lambda^{1/5}<6/5$. The remaining term is below $(4/15)(6/5)^2=48/125$, so $S'/S<25/49+48/125<9/10$.

These cases cover the normalized strip. If the central region fails, one coordinate exceeds $4/5$: a coordinate below $-4/5$ would, by $z+\zeta\ge0$, force bias magnitude greater than one. When $b\ge0$, either both coordinates are at least $3/10$, or the smaller is at most $3/10$ and a $K$ case applies. When $b\le0$, a coordinate below $-1/5$ forces the other below $4/5$ by the bias strip, putting both in the central region. Undo the temporary shift as in step 3.1 and repeat. Each iteration reduces $S$ by $9/10$, so after $O(\log H)$ iterations $S<15$, since initially $S\le2H^2$. For a determinant-one ellipse, its area-to-box ratio is $\pi/(4\sqrt{1+b^2})$: its area is $\pi$ and box half-widths are $\sqrt d,\sqrt a$ when the matrix is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\b&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Thus the final ratios exceed $\pi/16>1/6$. The inverse cumulative map is the desired $G$, including translated centers.

To control integer parts, after every contraction balance the top-left coefficients $a,\alpha$ using a right action $L^r$ with $\lambda^{-2}\le(a/\alpha)\lambda^{4r}\le\lambda^2$; this preserves skew. Let $T$ be the cumulative lattice map. Each column $v$ has some nonzero coordinate in $2^{-1/2}\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$, so $\|v\|^2\|v^\bullet\|^2\ge1/4$ by its nonzero rational norm, whose absolute value is at least $1/2$. Hence $a\alpha\ge H^{-2}/4$, and likewise $d\delta\ge H^{-2}/4$. Since $(ad)(\alpha\delta)=(1+b^2)(1+\beta^2)\le(1+2H^2)^2$, both products are also at most $4H^2(1+2H^2)^2$. Balancing makes $a,\alpha$ individually $H^{O(1)}$ and bounded below by $H^{-O(1)}$; $d=(1+b^2)/a$ and $\delta=(1+\beta^2)/\alpha$ have the same bounds. The quadratic forms then bound the entries of $T,T^\bullet$ by $H^{O(1)}$. At each iteration the temporary shifts and powers in step 3.1 and step 4.1 and step 4.2 and step 4.3 and step 4.4 have exponents $O(\log H)$ and values $H^{O(1)}$ as well. Integer parts are therefore computable by binary search within integer bounds $H^{O(1)}$ in $O(\log H)$ comparisons each. Balancing does not alter any skew estimate or termination bound, proving the quantitative claims without a free floor oracle.

citations.quote: Put $\lambda=1+\sqrt2$. For bounded closed real intervals $I,J$, let $N$ count $\alpha\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$ with $\alpha\in I$, $\alpha^\bullet\in J$, and put $P=|I||J|$. There is an explicit finite proposal list containing every solution once, with constant work per proposal, of length $O(N+1)$. If both lengths are positive its length is $O(P+1)$, and $N\ge P/(4\lambda^3)$ when $P\ge4\lambda^3$. The list has constant-size random-access data. Empty intervals give empty lists; singleton intervals are also allowed. Floor operations are specified as integer-part operations, and their comparison cost is charged separately, rather than assumed constant.

Let $E,F$ be ellipses in $\mathbb R^2$, specified by their centers and positive definite symmetric matrices. Normalize their matrices separately to determinant one, obtaining $D_0,\Delta_0$. Suppose the eigenvalues of both normalized matrices lie in $[H^{-1},H]$, $H\ge2$. There is a constructive real linear map $G$ such that $G\mathbb Z[\omega]=\mathbb Z[\omega]$, $\det G=\pm1$, $(Gu)^\bullet=G^\bullet u^\bullet$, and both $G(E)$ and $G^\bullet(F)$ have area at least $1/6$ of their axis-aligned bounding-box area. It uses $O(\log H)$ matrix/arithmetic/logarithm/exponentiation operations and $O(\log H)$ integer-part operations. All real quantities to which integer parts are applied have magnitude $H^{O(1)}$, so implementing those parts by comparisons and binary search costs $O((\log H)^2)$ operations overall. The entries of $G,G^\bullet$ have magnitude $H^{O(1)}$.

Let $\bullet$ be the automorphism of $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$ defined in
[[def-qc-cyclotomic-bullet-automorphism]], so $\omega^\bullet=-\omega=\omega^5$,
and let $u\in D\setminus\{0\}$ satisfy
$|u|\le1$ and $|u^\bullet|\le1$. Then $k=\operatorname{sde}(u)\ge0$. If
$a=(\sqrt2)^ku=a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3$, then

$$|a_j|\le2^{k/2}\quad(0\le j\le3).$$

Thus for each fixed $k$ only finitely many coefficient vectors can occur; the
integer search may be restricted to
$|a_j|\le\lfloor2^{k/2}\rfloor$.

Let $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, where $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The class $[5]_8$ is a
unit modulo $8$, so the cyclotomic Galois group supplier
[[cor-the-galois-group-of-a-rational-cyclotomic-field]] gives the unique
$\mathbb Q$-automorphism $\bullet$ with
$\omega^\bullet=\omega^5=-\omega$. It fixes $i=\omega^2$ and sends
$\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ to $-\sqrt2$. Complex conjugation and $\bullet$
commute, as is checked on the generator $\omega$. The four embeddings of $K$
are the identity, complex conjugation, $\bullet$, and their composite,
because the Galois group consists of the four maps $\omega\mapsto\omega^j$
for $j=1,3,5,7$. Since $\bullet$ fixes $1/2$ and maps $\omega$ into
$\mathbb Z[\omega]$, it preserves $D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$.

This is the nontrivial real-conjugation embedding used in the scaled-grid
conditions; it is distinct from complex conjugation.

derivations.claim: The ring $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$ has exactly four residue classes modulo $\sqrt2 O$, represented by $0,1,\omega,1+\omega$. Indeed $\sqrt2\omega=1+i$ and $\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ imply $i\equiv1$, $\omega^3\equiv\omega$, and $2\equiv0$. Conversely the coefficient map $a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3\mapsto(a_0+a_2,a_1+a_3)\bmod2$ annihilates every multiple of $\sqrt2$: multiplying by $\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ gives even sums in both coordinates. Thus those four residues are distinct and exhaustive. Consequently for $k\ge1$ the three chosen affine subproblems describe precisely the elements of least exponent $k$. For $k=0$, the algorithm scans all $81$ coefficient tuples in $\{-1,0,1\}^4$; [F3] bounds every nonzero grid candidate in this layer by that box, and zero fails the cap because $1-\varepsilon^2/2>0$. The two further cosets $\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]+i\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$ and its translate by $\omega$ partition $O$: expand a power-basis element's real and imaginary parts and separate the parity of $a_1+a_3$. Thus all affine subproblems are disjoint. The lattice bijection [F2] and the exact filters preserve every solution, while the emitted set suppresses revisits. The exhaustive background scan makes every finite layer terminate for every sequence of random bits.

The cap is sandwiched between $E$ and its concentric $1/8$-dilate. In coordinates $u=xw+y iw$, cap points have $1-h\le x\le1$ and $y^2\le2h$, so $(x-(1-h/2))^2/h^2+y^2/(4h)\le1/4+1/2<1$. Conversely the $1/8$-ellipse lies in $|x-(1-h/2)|\le h/8$, $|y|\le\sqrt h/4$, hence $x\ge1-h$ and $x^2+y^2\le(1-3h/8)^2+h/16<1$ for $0<h<1/8$. The normalized outer ellipse eigenvalues are $2/\sqrt h$ and $\sqrt h/2$, within $[H^{-1},H]$ for $H=4/\varepsilon$; the disk matrix is the identity. Therefore [F2] applies with $\log H=O(L)$. For a final normalized ellipse matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\b&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with $b^2\le15$, its centered bounding box has half-widths $\sqrt d,\sqrt a$. At its box scaled by $1/8$, the quadratic form is at most $2(ad+|b|\sqrt{ad})/64\le1$, since $ad=1+b^2\le16$. Each transformed cap therefore contains its outer ellipse's bounding box scaled concentrically by $1/64$, and the same weaker bound holds for the transformed disk. Affine shifts, negative scalar dilations, and coset translations preserve these inclusions.

At $k=0$ the direct coefficient scan has at most $81$ proposals, hence $M=O(N+1)$ for the number $N$ of layer solutions. For $k\ge1$, consider one of the at most six subproblems. If $P_x,P_y\ge T$, the two inner axis rectangles from step 1.2 supply independent coordinate grid problems with length products $P_x/64^2$ and $P_y/64^2$. Both exceed $4\lambda^3$, so [F1] gives at least $cP_x$ and $cP_y$ solutions, with a fixed $c>0$. Their Cartesian product lies inside both true constraints, giving $N_{\rm sub}\ge c^2P_xP_y$. The two outer one-dimensional proposal lengths are $O(P_x+1)$ and $O(P_y+1)$, so their product is $O(N_{\rm sub})$. If one coordinate product is below $T$, its entire proposal list and filtered coordinate list have bounded length by [F1]. Each remaining exact slice gives $O(N_x+1)$ proposals by the same result, including singleton slices. Summing over the constantly many coordinate solutions gives $O(N_{\rm sub}+1)$ proposals. Combining the at most six disjoint subproblems proves $M=O(N+1)$. In particular an empty layer has only constantly many proposals; no exponentially large lower-denominator list is generated.

The bound [F2] on $G$ and the affine scalings $2^{k/2}$ bounds all outer centers and widths above by $\exp(O(k+L))$. A nonzero outer width is bounded below by $\exp(-O(k+L))$, by the ellipse eigenvalue bounds and $\det G=\pm1$. Thus the integer parts in outer one-dimensional preprocessing cost $O(k+L)$ comparisons each. There are only constantly many exact slice intervals in the small-coordinate branch. A positive slice can have arbitrarily small width, so the algorithm pads it before the [F1] normalization: replace a slice width $\delta$ smaller than $1/(\Delta+1)$ by that value, keeping its center and filtering the original slice. Its product is at most one and it creates constantly many proposals. Otherwise $\delta\ge1/(\Delta+1)$, so both positive widths used for normalization are at least $\exp(-O(k+L))$, since $\Delta$ is bounded by the outer width. The same padding handles singleton slices, and an empty slice is skipped. In either branch the [F1] unit-rescaling exponents are $O(k+L)$, all floor operands have magnitude $\exp(O(k+L))$, and the earlier $O(N_x+1)$ bound is retained. Root and line-intersection calculations use boundedly many source arithmetic operations; sign decisions are charged exact comparisons. Finally $M=O(N+1)$ and [F3] give $\log(M+1)=O(k+1)$, so each random proposal attempt uses $O(k+1)$ random bits and is accepted with probability at least $1/2$. A balanced comparison tree on exact coefficient tuples handles the emitted set in $O(\log(N+2))=O(k+1)$ comparisons per visit. Thus each proposal visit and all layer preprocessing cost $\operatorname{poly}(k+L)$ in expectation, with polynomial moments.

Every actual solution occupies exactly one proposal index. For $N\ge1$, after $s<N$ distinct solutions have been drawn, an independent random attempt produces a new solution with probability at least $(N-s)/(2M)$. Ignoring the background scan can only delay obtaining $j$ solutions. The expected number of random draws to obtain them is at most $\sum_{s<j}2M/(N-s)\le2C(N+1)\sum_{s<j}1/(N-s)\le4Cj\sum_{t=1}^j1/t$, since $N/(N-s)\le j/(j-s)$ for $N\ge j$. This is $O(j(1+\log j))$. Moreover each waiting time is dominated by a geometric variable with success probability $1/(4C(s+1))$, whose $r$th moment is $O_r((s+1)^r)$: sum its geometric tail, or bound the sum by the integral of $r x^{r-1}\exp(-x/(4C(s+1)))$. The inequality $(\sum_{s<j}x_s)^r\le j^{r-1}\sum_{s<j}x_s^r$ gives the stated $O_r(j^{2r})$ draw-moment bound. Each random draw adds only one background visit. Independently, after at most $M$ such pairs the deterministic scan ends the layer, bounding complete-layer work by $O((N+1)\operatorname{poly}(k+L))$. Combining these estimates with step 3.1 proves all complexity claims. They control prefixes as well as complete output sizes, so they do not hide a whole-layer precomputation before the first candidate.

citations.quote:
Fix $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$ and $D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$. Use the automorphism
$\bullet$ from [[def-qc-cyclotomic-bullet-automorphism]], which sends
$\omega$ to $-\omega=\omega^5$ and fixes $i$. Let $0<\varepsilon<1/2$ and
$\theta\in\mathbb R$. The scaled grid for this input is

$$\mathcal G(\theta,\varepsilon)=\{u\in D:\ |u|\le1,\ |u^\bullet|\le1,\ \operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)\ge1-\varepsilon^2/2\}.$$

The default iterator is [[alg-qc-rz-efficient-scaled-grid-iterator]], with
$w=e^{-i\theta/2}$. It emits every candidate once in increasing least
$k=\operatorname{sde}(u)$, with randomized order within each layer and
finite layer completion for every random-bit sequence. Its expected prefix
cost and all fixed prefix moments are proved in
[[thm-qc-rz-efficient-scaled-grid-enumeration]].

A complete finite-search alternative uses lexicographic power-basis
coefficients within each layer. For each $k\ge0$, write
$u=(a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3)/(\sqrt2)^k$ with least exponent
$k$; the finite coefficient bound is
$|a_j|\le\lfloor2^{k/2}\rfloor$, proved in
[[lem-qc-cyclotomic-scaled-grid-finiteness]]. Test the three displayed
conditions exactly. This defines a finite candidate list for each $k$.

For a candidate $u$, put
$\xi=1-u^\dagger u=1-|u|^2\in D_+=\mathbb Z[\sqrt2,1/2]$, using
[[lem-qc-dyadic-cyclotomic-conjugate-norm]]. For scalars, $z^\dagger=\bar z$.
Write
$\xi^\bullet\xi=n/2^\ell$ with $n\in\mathbb Z$ and least $\ell\ge0$; compute
it by writing $\xi=a+b\sqrt2$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Z[1/2]$ and multiplying
$(a-b\sqrt2)(a+b\sqrt2)=a^2-2b^2$. The two disk conditions give
$\xi,\xi^\bullet\ge0$, so $n\ge0$; if $\xi\ne0$, injectivity of $\bullet$
gives $n>0$.
The complete norm-equation subprocedure receives $\xi$ and, if $n\ne0$, a prime
factorization of $n$. It must decide whether some $t\in D$ satisfies
$t^\dagger t=\xi$, return an exact such $t$ if one exists, and otherwise return
`NO_SOLUTION`. If $\xi=0$, it returns $t=0$. A bounded factorization attempt
may return `FACTOR_TIMEOUT`; that result skips this candidate and is not a
proof of `NO_SOLUTION`.

### Factored norm-equation subprocedure

When the supplied integer factorization is available, use the efficient
construction in [[thm-qc-factored-cyclotomic-norm-equation-efficient]].
Clear the denominator by $\eta=4^r\xi$, taking the least nonnegative
$r$ for which $\eta\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$. For each rational prime in its
known norm factorization, recover its real prime generators using
$\gcd(p,\sqrt2-b)$ when $b^2=2\pmod p$ exists, and otherwise retain
$p$. Split these into cyclotomic prime generators by the displayed modular
roots of $-1$ or $-2$ and cyclotomic gcds; retain the inert generators and
include $\delta=1+\omega$ over $2$. Recover the exponents in
$\eta$ by exact division, allocate them under complex conjugation as below,
and recover the real unit by multiplying by $1+\sqrt2$ or its inverse
until its positive embedding lies in $[1,1+\sqrt2)$.
The cited construction specifies all residue-class branches and its
randomized modular square-root subroutine; balance gcd remainders by real
units as there. It returns an exact solution or `NO_SOLUTION` and has
expected polynomial bit cost in the explicit algebraic input size. For a
grid candidate of exponent $k$, this is polynomial in $k+1$.

### Calibrated bounded prime attempts

In bounded mode no prime recognition oracle is used. For candidate exponent
$k$, use the fixed calibrated polynomial
$$P(k)=2^{200}(k+1)^{20}$$
from [[thm-qc-factored-cyclotomic-norm-equation-efficient]]. If $n=0$,
return $t=0$. If $n=1$, run the complete efficient construction with the
empty odd-prime factor list; its remaining powers of two are known.

For $n>1$, execute the factored construction prospectively, using the
single factor hint $n^1$, for at most $2P(k)$ of its elementary binary
operations. This is an attempt, not a claim that $n$ is prime. Instrument
all loops, including random sampling, with this counter. Guard every partial
operation: check divisors for zero and obtain modular inverses by the
integer extended Euclidean algorithm, aborting if the gcd is not one.
Impossible order/root searches, malformed outputs, negative solver outcomes,
failed inverses, and work-cap interruptions all end the attempt with
`FACTOR_TIMEOUT`, never with a claim of `NO_SOLUTION`.

Before accepting any prospective output, reduce its rational power-basis
coefficients and check $t^\dagger t=\xi$ exactly. Accept only when that
equality holds; otherwise return `FACTOR_TIMEOUT`. Watchdog, guard and final
certificate costs are charged; they are polynomial in $k+1+P(k)$ even on
composite inputs. The solver-work counter bounds every intermediate bit
string by its input length plus $2P(k)$, so certification cannot hide an
unbounded output cost. Use fresh independent random bits at each candidate.

After the capped prime attempt fails, return FACTOR_TIMEOUT for this
candidate and continue to the next grid candidate. Bounded mode makes no
additional factoring attempt and takes no factor-suggestion procedure or
additional factor-attempt budget as input. Complete oracle mode instead
supplies a valid full factorization and runs the complete efficient solver
without this cap.

### Complete finite-search alternative

Use the complete terminating construction of
[[thm-qc-cyclotomic-norm-equation-decision]]. Explicitly, after the zero
case choose the least integer $r\ge0$ clearing the coefficient denominators so that
$\eta=4^r\xi\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$. Factor $\eta$ in
$O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$ by the finite divisor search in
[[lem-qc-cyclotomic-euclidean-factorization-and-units]]. Group the prime
associate classes under $\dagger$. If any fixed class has odd exponent,
return `NO_SOLUTION`. Otherwise form $s$ by allocating half each fixed
exponent, and all of the common exponent to one class from each conjugate
pair. Compute the positive real unit $e=\eta/(s^\dagger s)$, recover
$v\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$ with $v^2=e$ by the unit construction, and return
$t=vs/2^r$. Every computation here uses exact power-basis arithmetic.

The supplied integer factorization is retained as an admissible input for
implementations using rational-prime splitting. The finite-search mode above
does not need it and has no asserted polynomial runtime. In bounded mode,
FACTOR_TIMEOUT skips the current candidate and never changes the complete
subprocedure's NO_SOLUTION criterion.

### Comparison contract

The grid comparisons involve the supplied real parameters $\theta$ and
$\varepsilon$. Their exact comparison interface is part of the outer
real-input contract. It is independent of the algebraic norm solver, whose
sign, equality, divisibility and associate tests are all exact and terminating.

Put $R=\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$, $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$, and $D=O[1/2]$, with $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. Given $\xi\in R[1/2]$ and a valid complete rational-prime factorization of the nonzero numerator $n$ in the reduced fraction $\xi^\bullet\xi=n/2^\ell$, there is an exact randomized algorithm returning $t\in D$ with $t^\dagger t=\xi$, or correctly reporting that no such $t$ exists. Zero input requires no factorization. The algorithm terminates almost surely and has expected bit cost polynomial in the total binary length $L$ of the explicitly encoded rational coefficients of $\xi$ and the supplied factorization. Denominators are ordinary binary integers, not compressed exponent encodings. The algorithm does not compute or verify rational primality of the promised prime factors.

In particular, suppose $0\le\xi,\xi^\bullet\le1$, and $k$ is the least nonnegative integer with $(\sqrt2)^k\xi\in R$. Given the factorization of $n$, the expected cost, including exact solution recovery or a correct negative answer, is polynomial in $k+1$ when $\xi$ is supplied in reduced coefficient form. For a grid candidate $u\in D$ with least $\sqrt2$-denominator exponent $h$, its residual $\xi=1-u^\dagger u$ has least exponent at most $2h$. Under the same embedding bounds, $n\le4^h$ and the residual solver has expected cost polynomial in $h+1$. The unrestricted cost includes the bit length of the coefficients, rather than depending on $\log n$ alone.

For the stated grid residual with $n$ prime, or $n\in\{0,1\}$, a concrete schoolbook implementation of this algorithm has expected bit cost at most $P(h)=2^{200}(h+1)^{20}$. This explicit bound includes input reading in reduced coefficient form and exact verification of a returned solution. Bit cost counts Boolean operations and bit reads/writes on binary arrays; multi-bit arithmetic is performed by the schoolbook loops detailed below. It gives a numerical cap for interrupted attempts; it makes no correctness or termination assertion about calling prime-specific branches with a composite integer falsely presented as prime.

Let $u\in D$ satisfy $|u|,|u^\bullet|\le1$, put
$\xi=1-u^\dagger u$, and write $\xi^\bullet\xi=n/2^\ell$ with
$n\in\mathbb Z$ and least $\ell\ge0$. Then $n\ge0$, and either $n=0$ or
$n\equiv1\pmod8$. If $u\ne0$ has least square-root-of-two denominator
exponent $k$, then $n\le4^k$.

Let $\xi\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2,1/2]$ be positive at both real embeddings.
If $\xi^\bullet\xi=p/2^\ell$ with $\ell\ge0$ and a rational prime
$p\equiv1\pmod8$, then $t^\dagger t=\xi$ has a solution in
$\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$. The complete finite-time norm solver returns a
solution on every such input. The same conclusion holds when
$\xi^\bullet\xi=1/2^\ell$. No runtime bound is implied.

derivations.claim: The exact certificate check in [F1] is a comparison of the four rational power-basis coefficients of $t^\dagger t$ and $\xi$. Equality of these coefficients is equality in the field, so acceptance always proves the required equation. On a composite input no field property of a proposed residue quotient and no `NO_SOLUTION` message is used as evidence: a failed operation, negative outcome, or work-cap interruption causes only a skip.

The construction is interrupted after $B=2\lceil P(k)\rceil$ binary operations, regardless of whether its proposed prime factor was valid. Every generated bit string then has length bounded by the input length plus $B$. The grid-input bound of [F2] makes its input length polynomial in $k+1$. A fixed-degree rational-coefficient multiplication and equality check therefore takes polynomial work in $k+1+B$, by schoolbook integer multiplication and division. Since $B$ is a specified polynomial, total work including exact certification is polynomial on every input.

If $n$ is prime, the proposed one-factor factorization is valid, and [F3,F4] make its norm equation solvable. Let $T\ge0$ be the binary work of the uncapped construction on this input.
